title: The Syntopicon
subtitle: The 102 Great Ideas of the Western tradition
source: After Mortimer J. Adler & William Gorman, A Syntopicon: An Index to The Great Ideas (1952).
note: A study companion in the spirit of Adler's Syntopicon: for each idea, the senses a term takes, the live disputes and who holds each side, what thinkers argued, an outline of topics, and the primary texts to read. Framing and disputes are written for study -- faithful to the tradition, but not reproductions of Adler's essays or outlines. A guide toward the originals, not a substitute. This edition adds a biographical register of every thinker cited (dates, era and significance), dates for every primary text, and the famous lines associated with each idea together with the context that gives them their meaning.

clusters.blurb: Metaphysics and cosmology: what exists, and how.

clusters.name: The Divine & Last Things
clusters.blurb: Theology and the ultimate horizon of existence.

clusters.name: Mind, Knowledge & Method
clusters.blurb: How we know, reason, and err.

clusters.name: Nature & Life
clusters.blurb: The living world, the body, the cosmos, and man within it.

ideas.name: Angel
ideas.gist: A purely intellectual being: mind without a body.
ideas.framing: An angel is a purely spiritual, intelligent being -- a messenger without a body -- standing between God and man. Beyond theology, the angel is philosophy's test case for whether a mind can exist without matter, and how such a mind would know.
senses: Messenger of God (the scriptural sense)
Pure intelligence or separate substance (the philosophical sense)
A rank within the celestial hierarchy
Guardian and ministering spirit

disputes.q: Do purely spiritual beings exist?

sides.view: Separate intelligences without bodies exist
There is no incorporeal substance

disputes.q: Is each angel an individual, or a whole species?

sides.view: Each angel is its own species, since it has no matter to individuate it
Angels differ as individuals within kinds

disputes.q: How do angels know and act?

sides.view: By infused ideas and intuitive, not discursive, knowledge
Such claims exceed what can be known

positions.name: Pseudo-Dionysius
positions.claim: Sets out the celestial hierarchy of nine angelic orders.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: The separate intelligences that move the heavenly spheres are a philosophical ancestor of the angels.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Angels are subsistent forms without matter; each is its own species and knows by infused ideas.

positions.name: Milton
positions.claim: Dramatizes the angels, their war, and their fall in Paradise Lost.

topics: Angels and the motion of the heavens
ideas.example: Aquinas argues each angel is its own species because, having no matter to divide it, nothing could distinguish two angels of one kind.

quotes.text: Each angel is its own species.
quotes.context: A consequence of having no matter. Since Aquinas holds matter is what makes two things of one kind distinct individuals, purely spiritual beings cannot differ as individuals -- each must differ in kind.

ideas.name: Animal
ideas.gist: The living, sensing, moving creature—including and excluding man.
ideas.framing: The animal is the living, sentient being -- possessing soul, sensation, and self-motion, yet (for most of the tradition) lacking reason. It is the mirror in which humanity defines itself, and the test case for whether life and mind are more than mechanism.
senses: Any living, ensouled being (including man, the 'rational animal')
The sentient, self-moving creature (vs. plants)
The brute or beast (non-rational, contrasted with man)
The organism studied by biology

disputes.q: Do animals have reason or only sensation?

sides.view: Only sense, appetite, and imagination -- no reason
They show intelligence differing in degree, not kind

disputes.q: Are animals machines or ensouled?

sides.view: Mere automata, without thought or feeling
Sentient beings with a sensitive soul

disputes.q: Is man an animal like the rest?

sides.view: A distinct rational animal, set apart
One species continuous with the others

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Classifies animals by their powers of soul; the animal has sensation and self-motion, not reason.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: Animals are machines -- complex automata lacking thought or a rational soul.

positions.name: Montaigne
positions.claim: Mocks human presumption, arguing beasts show cunning, communication, and feeling.

positions.name: Darwin
positions.claim: Man differs from the higher animals in degree, not kind; mind itself has an animal ancestry.

key_texts.text: Aristotle, History of Animals; On the Soul

ideas.example: Aristotle's ladder of souls gives plants nutrition, animals sensation and movement, and humans reason atop both.
ideas.hook: The body that feels and moves.

quotes.text: Animals are machines.
quotes.context: The beast-machine doctrine. Lacking language and reason, animals are automata however complex their behavior -- a position Montaigne had already ridiculed and which troubled even Descartes' followers.

ideas.name: Aristocracy
ideas.gist: Rule by the best—and the problem of who they are.
ideas.framing: Aristocracy is rule by the best -- government by a select few distinguished by virtue or excellence. As one of the classic forms of government, it raises the question whether the wisest and best should rule, and how they are to be identified.
senses: Rule of the best or most virtuous (the ideal sense)
Rule of the few (contrasted with the many)
A hereditary nobility (the historical sense)
'Natural aristocracy' of talent vs. aristocracy of birth

disputes.q: Who are 'the best' fit to rule?

sides.view: The truly virtuous and wise
In practice the wellborn and wealthy -- so it decays into oligarchy

disputes.q: Should the best rule, or the people?

sides.view: The wisest should govern for the common good
The people should rule themselves

disputes.q: Is aristocracy natural or a usurpation?

sides.view: A natural aristocracy of virtue is just
Hereditary privilege is arbitrary and unjust

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: The ideal city is ruled by philosopher-kings -- the few who know the good -- a true aristocracy of wisdom.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Aristocracy is rule of the few for the common good; it decays into oligarchy when the rich rule for themselves.

positions.name: Montesquieu
positions.claim: In aristocracy power rests with a body of nobles; its animating principle is moderation.

positions.name: Jefferson
positions.claim: Distinguishes a 'natural aristocracy' of virtue and talent from an artificial one of birth and wealth.

key_texts.text: Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws

ideas.example: Plato's guardians are bred, tested, and educated for decades so that only the genuinely wise reach the top—an attempt to make merit, not birth, the credential.
ideas.hook: The best rule—if you can find them.

quotes.text: A natural aristocracy of virtue and talents.
quotes.context: Distinguished from an artificial aristocracy founded on wealth and birth. Jefferson thought the best government provides for sorting the natural sort into office -- and blocking the artificial.

ideas.name: Art
ideas.gist: The made thing, and the human power of making by rule.
ideas.framing: Art is the making of things by skill according to a conception -- from craft to fine art. Whether art imitates nature, expresses its maker, or creates beauty, and what its value is, are questions running from Plato to the moderns.
senses: Skill or craft (techne -- any productive know-how)
Fine art (the arts of beauty)
The liberal arts vs. the mechanical or servile arts
Art as imitation (mimesis) vs. art as creation and expression

disputes.q: Does art imitate nature or create anew?

sides.view: Art imitates nature and reality
Art expresses the artist and creates a new world

disputes.q: Is art morally beneficial or dangerous?

sides.view: It can corrupt -- imitations feeding the passions
It instructs and purges the emotions

disputes.q: Is 'art' one thing?

sides.view: A single genus of skilled making
The fine arts are radically distinct from crafts

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Art imitates appearances, thrice removed from the Forms; the poets must be watched, even banished.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Art completes or imitates nature; tragedy imitates action and, through pity and fear, purges the emotions.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Fine art is the product of genius -- purposive yet free, pleasing without a concept.

positions.name: Tolstoy
positions.claim: Art is the communication of feeling; its worth lies in the sincerity and value of what it transmits.

topics: Art as skill and as fine art
ideas.example: A doctor practicing the 'art of medicine' and a sculptor practicing sculpture were, classically, doing the same kind of thing: making by rule.

quotes.text: Art imitates nature.
quotes.context: Not copying appearances. Art works as nature does -- toward an end, giving form to material -- and may complete what nature leaves unfinished, which is why he can defend the poets Plato banished.

ideas.name: Astronomy
ideas.gist: The oldest science: reading order in the heavens.
ideas.framing: Astronomy is the science of the heavens -- the motions of stars and planets and the structure of the cosmos. Its revolutions, from geocentric to heliocentric, reshaped not only physics but humanity's sense of its place.
senses: The mathematical account of celestial motions ('saving the appearances')
Cosmology -- the real structure of the universe
Observational vs. theoretical astronomy
Astronomy vs. astrology

disputes.q: Does the earth or the sun stand at the center?

sides.view: Geocentric -- the earth is fixed at the center
Heliocentric -- the earth moves about the sun

disputes.q: Do astronomical models describe reality or merely predict?

sides.view: Mere calculating devices to save the appearances
True descriptions of the heavens

disputes.q: Are the heavens a different matter from the earth?

sides.view: A perfect, changeless fifth element
The same physics rules heaven and earth

positions.name: Ptolemy
positions.claim: A geocentric system of epicycles and deferents that accurately predicts the planets' motions.

positions.name: Copernicus
positions.claim: Places the sun at the center, setting the earth in motion among the planets.

positions.name: Kepler
positions.claim: The planets travel in ellipses, sweeping equal areas in equal times.

positions.name: Galileo
positions.claim: Telescopic evidence -- Jupiter's moons, the phases of Venus -- supports the heliocentric cosmos.

positions.name: Newton
positions.claim: Universal gravitation explains celestial and terrestrial motion by one law.

topics: The size and structure of the cosmos

key_texts.text: Galileo, Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems

ideas.example: Kepler abandoned the perfect circle—sacred since antiquity—because Mars's orbit only fit an ellipse, letting data overrule beauty.

quotes.text: The book of nature is written in the language of mathematics.
quotes.context: A methodological manifesto: without geometry one wanders a dark labyrinth. It licenses treating measurable quantities as what is real and relegating qualities to the observer.

ideas.name: Beauty
ideas.gist: The quality that pleases when merely beheld.
ideas.framing: Beauty is that which pleases when perceived -- the splendor of form, order, and proportion. Whether beauty is a real property of things or lies in the eye of the beholder, and how it relates to the good and the true, are its central questions.
senses: Objective proportion, harmony, order (in the thing)
What pleases the beholder (in the response)
Sensible beauty vs. intelligible or moral beauty
Beauty and the sublime

disputes.q: Is beauty in the object or the beholder?

sides.view: A real feature -- proportion, harmony, radiance
A feeling in the subject -- no quality in things themselves

disputes.q: Is beauty objective or a matter of taste?

sides.view: There are real standards of taste and beauty
Taste is relative; to each his own

disputes.q: Is beauty the same as the good and the true?

sides.view: The beautiful, good, and true are one at the summit
Beauty is distinct -- a disinterested pleasure, not desire or use

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: The soul ascends from beautiful bodies to Beauty itself -- eternal, absolute, the object of love.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Beauty consists in order, symmetry, and definiteness, which the mathematical sciences reveal.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: The beautiful is 'that which pleases when seen'; it requires wholeness, proportion, and radiance.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: Beauty is no quality in things; it exists in the mind -- yet a standard of taste can be found.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: The judgment of beauty is a disinterested, universal pleasure in form, claiming all agreement without a concept.

topics: Beauty in the object vs. the beholder
Beauty and the good and true

key_texts.text: Aquinas, Summa Theologica I Q.5, Q.39
Hume, Of the Standard of Taste

ideas.example: Kant's test: your pleasure in a rose is aesthetic only if you'd want anyone to feel it too, yet can't prove they should—universal but not provable.

quotes.text: That which pleases when seen.
quotes.context: Beauty is close to the good, but distinguished from it: the good is what we desire and pursue, while the beautiful satisfies simply in the apprehending. He adds it requires wholeness, proportion and radiance.

ideas.name: Being
ideas.gist: That anything is at all—the root question.
ideas.framing: Being is the most universal and most puzzling of ideas: what it means for anything to be at all, and whether 'being' names one thing or many. It is the very subject of metaphysics, the science of being as being.
senses: Existence (that a thing is) vs. essence (what it is)
Being as substance vs. being as attribute or relation
Actual being vs. potential being
Being as the one vs. being as the many

disputes.q: Is being one or many?

sides.view: One changeless reality; plurality and change are illusion
Being is said in many ways; there are many beings and kinds of being

disputes.q: Is 'being' univocal or analogical?

sides.view: 'Being' means the same in every case
God and creatures 'are' in related but different senses (analogy)

disputes.q: Does becoming have being, or only what is permanent?

sides.view: Only the eternal Forms truly are; sensibles merely become
All is flux; being is becoming

positions.name: Parmenides
positions.claim: Being simply is, ungenerated and changeless; since not-being cannot be thought, change and plurality are illusory.

positions.name: Heraclitus
positions.claim: Reality is ceaseless becoming; you cannot step into the same river twice.

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: True being belongs to the eternal Forms; sensible things are shadows that partake of them.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Being is said in many ways but primarily of substance; a science of being as being studies its universal features.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: God is being itself (ipsum esse); creatures have being by participation, so essence and existence differ in them.

topics: Being as the object of metaphysics

key_texts.text: Aquinas, Summa Theologica I QQ.2-11; On Being and Essence

ideas.example: Parmenides argued that since 'what is not' can't even be thought, change—which needs a passage from not-being—must be illusion.
ideas.hook: That it is, before what it is.

quotes.text: Being is, and not-being is not.
quotes.context: The starting axiom of Western metaphysics. If nothing cannot be, then nothing can come from nothing, and change -- which needs something to pass into being -- becomes impossible. Every later account of change is a reply to this.

ideas.name: Cause
ideas.gist: Why things are and come to be as they do.
ideas.framing: A cause is that on which a thing depends for its being or its coming-to-be. The idea governs whether the world is intelligible -- whether things happen for reasons, by purpose, by mechanism, or merely in constant sequence.
senses: The four causes: material, formal, efficient, final
Cause as necessitating vs. cause as probabilistic
First cause vs. secondary causes
Cause as real power vs. cause as regular succession

disputes.q: How many kinds of cause are there?

sides.view: Four -- material, formal, efficient, final
Really only efficient (mechanical) causes; final causes are illusory in nature

disputes.q: Is there purpose (final cause) in nature?

sides.view: Nature acts for ends; teleology is real
Apparent purpose is the product of blind mechanism or selection

disputes.q: Can causation be observed?

sides.view: We perceive only constant conjunction and succession, never necessary connection
Causality is an a priori category the mind supplies to experience

disputes.q: Is there a first cause?

sides.view: An uncaused first cause is required to end the regress
The demand for a first cause is unprovable or illegitimate

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Distinguishes four causes and argues both nature and art act for ends; a prime mover is the first cause of motion.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Uses efficient causation and the impossibility of infinite regress to argue for God as first cause.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: We never observe the 'must'; causal belief is a habit born of repeated conjunction.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Cause-and-effect is a category structuring all possible experience, not derived from it.

positions.name: Mill
positions.claim: Causes are found by empirical methods of agreement and difference among phenomena.

topics: The efficient cause and the transmission of motion
The first cause and infinite regress
Cause in nature vs. cause in art

key_texts.text: Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding VII
Kant, Critique of Pure Reason (Second Analogy)

ideas.example: Hume noted that no matter how often the cue ball strikes the eight, we see only one motion then another—never the 'must' between them.

quotes.text: Nothing comes from nothing.
quotes.work: On the Nature of Things I
quotes.context: The Epicurean first principle, aimed against miracle and divine caprice: if things arose from nothing, anything could come from anything, and nature would show no regular kinds.

ideas.name: Chance
ideas.gist: The uncaused, the coincidental, the merely probable.
ideas.framing: Chance names what happens neither always nor for the most part, seemingly without cause or purpose. Whether chance is real or merely a mask for our ignorance shapes the whole question of order and design in the world.
senses: Chance as the coincidental (a cause outside intention)
Chance as pure randomness (uncaused)
Chance as our ignorance of hidden causes
Luck and fortune in human affairs

disputes.q: Is chance real or only apparent?

sides.view: Chance is real: the coincidence of independent causal lines
Nothing happens by chance; 'chance' names causes we do not know

disputes.q: Does randomness operate in nature?

sides.view: Random variation is a genuine factor (mutation, drift)
Apparent randomness reduces to strict law at bottom

disputes.q: Can chance be quantified?

sides.view: Yes -- probability turns chance into calculable degrees
Probability measures our ignorance, not chance in things

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Chance is the coincidental intersection of purposive or natural processes -- real but parasitic on regular causes.

positions.name: Epicurus
positions.claim: Adds a random 'swerve' to the fall of atoms to break the chain of necessity.

positions.name: The Stoics
positions.claim: Fate rules all; nothing is by chance, only by our failure to see the cause.

positions.name: Laplace
positions.claim: An intelligence knowing all forces could predict everything; chance is merely ignorance.

positions.name: Darwin
positions.claim: Chance variation supplies the raw material that natural selection shapes.

key_texts.text: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things
Laplace, A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities

ideas.example: Aristotle's example: a man goes to market for bread and, by chance, meets a debtor who repays him—two purposeful paths crossing without either intending the meeting.
ideas.hook: Causal lines that cross by accident.

quotes.text: The swerve.
quotes.work: On the Nature of Things II
quotes.context: The Epicurean device to save freedom: atoms falling through the void deviate slightly at no fixed time or place. Without it, everything would be fixed by prior collisions and the will would be a link in an unbroken chain.

ideas.name: Change
ideas.gist: The passage from one state to another—and whether it is real.
ideas.framing: Change is the passage from one state to another -- the most obvious fact of experience and the hardest to make intelligible. To explain change is to explain how a thing can become what it was not while remaining itself.
senses: Change of place (locomotion)
Change of quality (alteration)
Change of quantity (growth and diminution)
Coming-to-be and passing-away (substantial change)

disputes.q: Is change real?

sides.view: Change is impossible; being cannot come from not-being
Change is the fundamental reality
Change is real, explained by potency and act

disputes.q: What underlies change?

sides.view: An enduring substratum (matter) persists through change
Only successive states or events; no enduring substance needed

disputes.q: Is change reducible to motion of parts?

sides.view: All qualitative change reduces to local motion of matter
Some change is genuinely qualitative or substantial

positions.name: Heraclitus
positions.claim: All things flow; strife and flux are the very law of the world.

positions.name: Parmenides
positions.claim: What is, is; motion and change are illusion -- as Zeno's paradoxes press.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Change is the actualizing of a potentiality; it requires matter, form, and privation.

positions.name: Newton
positions.claim: Change of motion is proportional to impressed force; nature's changes fall under laws of motion.

positions.name: Hegel
positions.claim: Reality develops dialectically; change through contradiction is the engine of the real.

topics: Motion as a species of change
ideas.example: Aristotle's acorn resolves the old paradox: it is actually an acorn but potentially an oak, so becoming an oak is potency made actual, not being from non-being.

quotes.text: No man steps in the same river twice.
quotes.context: Often quoted as pure flux, but the point is subtler: the river persists as a river precisely by its waters always changing. Identity is maintained through change, not destroyed by it.

ideas.name: Citizen
ideas.gist: The member of a political community, ruling and ruled in turn.
ideas.framing: The citizen is the member of a political community who shares in its rule and its rights. What makes one a citizen, what citizens owe and are owed, and who is included or excluded are foundational questions of political life.
senses: One who shares in ruling and being ruled (the participatory sense)
One holding legal rights and status (the juridical sense)
Citizen vs. subject (active member vs. one merely ruled)
Citizen vs. alien or slave (the included vs. the excluded)

disputes.q: What defines a citizen?

sides.view: Sharing in the offices and judgments of the city
Holding legal rights and protections

disputes.q: Who should be citizens?

sides.view: Only those with the leisure and virtue to rule well
All who are subject to the laws

disputes.q: Do citizens owe primary loyalty to the state?

sides.view: The citizen is part of the whole, owing devotion
Individuals have rights prior to the state, which serves them

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: The citizen is one who shares in ruling and being ruled in turn; citizenship varies with the constitution.

positions.name: The Romans
positions.claim: Develop citizenship as a legal status with defined rights, extendable across an empire.

positions.name: Rousseau
positions.claim: The citizen participates in the general will; sovereignty belongs to the assembled people.

positions.name: Modern liberalism
positions.claim: Citizenship is equal legal membership, securing rights even against the state.

topics: The rights and duties of citizens
Who is included as a citizen
ideas.example: Aristotle defines the citizen not by residence but by eligibility to hold office and sit in judgment—so a resident alien or laborer, present but excluded, was not a citizen.
ideas.hook: Ruler and ruled in one person.

quotes.text: Ruling and being ruled in turn.
quotes.context: His definition of the citizen, and why citizenship differs under different constitutions. It also frames civic virtue: one must learn obedience to be fit to command.

ideas.name: Constitution
ideas.gist: The ordering form of a state—its arrangement of powers.
ideas.framing: A constitution is the ordering of a state -- the arrangement of its offices, the distribution of power, and the way of life it embodies. It is at once the political structure and the fundamental law by which a people governs itself.
senses: The arrangement of offices and form of government (who rules and how)
The fundamental or higher law (a written or unwritten frame)
The whole 'way of life' or character of a community
The mixed constitution (blending forms)

disputes.q: Is a constitution just a structure, or a way of life?

sides.view: The arrangement of the ruling offices
The whole ethos and character of the community

disputes.q: What is the best constitution?

sides.view: The rule of the best or of philosopher-kings
A mixed constitution balancing the one, few, and many

disputes.q: Should the fundamental law be fixed or changeable?

sides.view: A stable higher law binding even the rulers
A living frame the people may amend

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Classifies constitutions by who rules and for whose good; the best practical form is a mixed 'polity.'

positions.name: Polybius
positions.claim: Praises the Roman mixed constitution, balancing consuls, senate, and people to slow decay.

positions.name: Montesquieu
positions.claim: Liberty is secured by the separation of powers -- legislative, executive, judicial.

positions.name: The Federalist
positions.claim: A written constitution with checks, balances, and divided powers guards against tyranny.

topics: Constitution and the way of life

key_texts.text: Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws

ideas.example: Polybius credited Rome's strength to mixing monarchy (consuls), aristocracy (senate), and democracy (assemblies) so each checked the others.
ideas.hook: The form that shapes the state.

quotes.text: A constitution is the way of life of a city.
quotes.context: Wider than a legal document. A constitution arranges the offices, but in doing so sets what the community honors and how its citizens live -- which is why changing it changes the people.

ideas.name: Courage
ideas.gist: Firmness of will in the face of fear and danger.
ideas.framing: Courage is the virtue of facing danger, fear, and pain for the sake of a good -- steadiness of will where much is at risk. Long counted a cardinal virtue, it presses the question of what is worth risking and how fear and confidence should be governed.
senses: Fortitude in battle or physical danger
Moral courage -- standing for the right against opposition
Endurance of pain and adversity
The mean between cowardice and rashness

disputes.q: Is courage knowledge or a trained passion?

sides.view: A kind of knowledge of what is and is not to be feared
A trained disposition of the spirited part, a mean

disputes.q: Does true courage require a good cause?

sides.view: Only a noble end makes daring courageous
Mere fearlessness or daring already counts

disputes.q: Is courage one virtue or bound up with all?

sides.view: Inseparable from wisdom -- the virtues are one
A distinct virtue among others

positions.name: Socrates
positions.claim: In the Laches, courage looks like a kind of wisdom -- knowledge of what is truly to be feared and dared.

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Courage is the spirited part's preservation of reason's judgment about what to fear.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Courage is the mean between cowardice and rashness, shown above all in facing a noble death.

positions.name: The Stoics
positions.claim: Courage is reason's endurance, unmoved by what is not truly evil.

topics: The mean between cowardice and rashness
ideas.example: Aristotle notes the truly brave soldier feels fear—the fearless one is merely reckless; courage is acting rightly while afraid.

quotes.text: Knowledge of what is and is not to be feared.
quotes.context: The definition the dialogue tests. If courage is knowledge it collapses into wisdom generally, which the Laches leaves unresolved -- an early case for the unity of the virtues.

ideas.name: Custom and Convention
ideas.gist: The unwritten rules that nature does not fix.
ideas.framing: Custom and convention are the settled but unwritten rules of a community -- what is done, expected, and agreed. Whether they rest on nature or mere agreement, and how far they bind, shapes debates over law, morality, and progress.
senses: Custom as habitual practice (the ways of a people)
Convention as agreement or posit (nomos, vs. physis, nature)
Customary law (unwritten but binding) vs. enacted law
Convention as arbitrary vs. as accumulated wisdom

disputes.q: Nature or convention -- which grounds right?

sides.view: Justice and morality are natural, above convention
They are conventional, mere human agreement

disputes.q: Is custom binding, or to be questioned?

sides.view: Custom carries the wisdom of ages and rightly guides us
Custom is often mere prejudice, to be tested by reason

disputes.q: Are conventions arbitrary or grounded?

sides.view: Purely arbitrary -- they could be otherwise
They solve real problems and embody experience

positions.name: The Sophists
positions.claim: Draw the great antithesis of nomos (convention) and physis (nature); much that seems just is merely conventional.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Some justice is natural, the same everywhere; some is legal and conventional, varying by place.

positions.name: Montaigne
positions.claim: Marvels at the diversity of customs, warning we mistake our own habits for nature's law.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: Justice and property are 'artificial' conventions -- yet indispensable, and not arbitrary.

positions.name: Burke
positions.claim: Custom and prescription embody the tacit wisdom of generations; reformers scorn them at their peril.

key_texts.text: Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France

ideas.example: Herodotus tells of Darius asking Greeks and Indians to adopt each other's funeral customs; both were horrified—showing how custom masquerades as nature.

quotes.text: Nature and convention.
quotes.context: The distinction that opened moral philosophy: are justice and law rooted in nature, or merely agreed and therefore changeable? Nearly every later ethical position takes a stand on it.

quotes.text: We call barbarism whatever is not our own practice.
quotes.context: Written after meeting Brazilians brought to France. Montaigne's point is not that all customs are equal but that we judge by habit and mistake familiarity for nature.

ideas.name: Definition
ideas.gist: Saying what a thing is—fixing the boundary of a concept.
ideas.framing: A definition states what a thing is -- fixing the meaning of a term or the essence of a thing. It is the starting point of demonstration and the arena where disputes over essences, words, and clarity are fought.
senses: Nominal definition (meaning of a word) vs. real definition (essence of a thing)
Definition by genus and specific difference
Ostensive definition (by pointing)
Stipulative vs. lexical definition

disputes.q: Do definitions capture real essences or only word-use?

sides.view: Real definitions state the essences of things
Definitions are of names only; we reach nominal essences

disputes.q: Can the most basic terms be defined?

sides.view: The first and simplest terms are indefinable
All can in principle be analyzed

disputes.q: Is definition the start of inquiry or its result?

sides.view: We must first ask 'What is it?'
Definition is the hard-won end of investigation

positions.name: Socrates
positions.claim: Presses the 'What is it?' question, seeking the single form common to all instances.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Real definition states the essence by genus and difference and grounds demonstration.

positions.name: Hobbes
positions.claim: Definitions are of names; 'truth consists in the right ordering of names.'

positions.name: Locke
positions.claim: We define the nominal essences (our ideas), not the hidden real essences of things.

ideas.example: Aristotle's 'man is a rational animal' defines by placing man in a genus (animal) and naming the difference (rational) that marks him within it.

quotes.text: Truth consists in the right ordering of names.
quotes.context: A radical nominalism. Truth belongs to propositions rather than things, so definitions are stipulations about words -- which is why Hobbes insists on settling them before reasoning begins.

ideas.name: Democracy
ideas.gist: Rule by the people—and the question of the many's competence.
ideas.framing: Democracy is rule by the people -- government in which the many, or all, share sovereign power. Praised as the reign of freedom and equality and feared as the tyranny of the majority, it is the most contested of political forms.
senses: Rule of the many or the people (the classic sense)
Direct (the assembled people) vs. representative democracy
Majority rule vs. the protection of rights
A form of government vs. a whole way of life and equality

disputes.q: Is democracy good or corrupt?

sides.view: A perverted form -- rule of the poor many for themselves
The best or only legitimate government -- self-rule of a free people

disputes.q: Should the majority rule without limit?

sides.view: The will of the people is sovereign
Majorities can tyrannize; rights must limit them

disputes.q: Is equality democracy's strength or danger?

sides.view: Equal participation is just and ennobling
Leveling equality breeds mediocrity and despotism

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Ranks democracy low -- liberty becomes license, and the disordered city slides toward tyranny.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Democracy is rule by the many (usually the poor); a moderate 'polity' mixing it with oligarchy is more stable.

positions.name: Rousseau
positions.claim: Legitimate rule expresses the general will; sovereignty belongs inalienably to the people.

positions.name: Tocqueville
positions.claim: Democratic equality is providential and just, yet risks the 'tyranny of the majority' and soft despotism.

positions.name: Mill
positions.claim: Representative democracy is the best government, but must protect individual liberty against the majority.

topics: The dangers and defenses of democracy
ideas.example: Tocqueville admired American equality yet warned that a majority can crush dissent more completely than any king, since it claims to speak for all.

quotes.text: The tyranny of the majority.
quotes.context: His warning that democratic despotism need not come from a ruler. When the majority's opinion carries moral as well as legal weight, dissent is silenced by social pressure rather than by force.

ideas.name: Desire
ideas.gist: The reaching of the soul toward what it lacks.
ideas.framing: Desire is the movement of the soul toward what it lacks and finds good -- the spring of action and the root of both fulfillment and disorder. Whether desire should be satisfied, guided, or extinguished is a central ethical question.
senses: Appetite for a sensible good (hunger, thirst, lust)
The rational will's wish for the good
Longing or eros (for beauty, the good, the divine)
Natural vs. vain (unnecessary) desires

disputes.q: Should desire be indulged, disciplined, or extinguished?

sides.view: Moderate and order it
Limit it to the natural and necessary
Extirpate the passions

disputes.q: Is desire always for the good?

sides.view: We desire only what appears good
We can desire the bad against our own judgment

disputes.q: Is desire the master or servant of reason?

sides.view: Reason should rule appetite
Reason is the slave of the passions

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Desire (appetite) is one part of the soul, to be ruled by reason with the help of spirit.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Rational desire (wish) aims at the good; virtue trains appetite to obey reason.

positions.name: Epicurus
positions.claim: Classifies desires; happiness lies in satisfying only the natural and necessary.

positions.name: The Stoics
positions.claim: Disordered desire is a false judgment; the sage is free of the passions.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: Reason alone moves no one; desire is the ultimate spring of action.

ideas.example: Plato's chariot has reason as charioteer struggling to control two horses—noble spirit and unruly appetite—a picture of desire needing government.
ideas.hook: The soul reaching for what it lacks.

quotes.text: Reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions.
quotes.context: Deliberately provocative. Reason establishes facts and means, but cannot by itself move anyone to act; only desire supplies ends. Kant's ethics is largely an answer to this.

ideas.name: Dialectic
ideas.gist: Reasoning by dialogue, opposition, and ascent.
ideas.framing: Dialectic is the art of reasoning through dialogue and opposition -- questioning, refuting, drawing distinctions to reach truth. Its meaning shifts sharply: the ascent to the Forms, mere probable argument, or the logic of contradiction that drives history.
senses: Socratic dialectic (question, answer, refutation)
Platonic dialectic (the ascent to the Forms)
Aristotelian dialectic (reasoning from accepted opinions, below demonstration)
Hegelian dialectic (development through contradiction)

disputes.q: Does dialectic yield knowledge or only the probable?

sides.view: It is the highest science, of the Forms
It reasons from mere opinions, beneath demonstration

disputes.q: Is dialectic a method of thought or a law of reality?

sides.view: A mode of argument
The very structure of reality and history

disputes.q: Is dialectic discovery or mere disputation?

sides.view: A path to truth
Eristic word-battling

positions.name: Socrates
positions.claim: By question and refutation (elenchus) he exposes ignorance and clears the way to knowledge.

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Dialectic ascends from hypotheses to the unhypothetical first principle, the Form of the Good.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Dialectic reasons from generally accepted opinions -- useful, but distinct from demonstration.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: 'Transcendental dialectic' exposes the illusions reason falls into beyond experience.

positions.name: Hegel
positions.claim: Dialectic is the movement by which contradictions are overcome in a higher unity.

topics: Dialectic as the logic of illusion
ideas.example: Hegel's master and slave: the master's dominance undoes itself because he comes to depend on the slave's recognition—a contradiction that drives history forward.

quotes.text: Thesis, antithesis, synthesis.
quotes.context: The famous summary Hegel himself never used in this form. What he does describe is a movement in which a position generates its own contradiction and both are preserved and overcome in something fuller.

ideas.name: Duty
ideas.gist: What is owed—action commanded regardless of desire.
ideas.framing: Duty is what one is morally bound to do -- obligation owed regardless of inclination or advantage. Whether morality is fundamentally about duty, and where duties come from, distinguishes the major ethical traditions.
senses: Moral obligation (what one ought to do)
The duties of one's station or role
Duty to law and country
Duty as the motive of moral worth (Kant)

disputes.q: Is morality grounded in duty or in the good?

sides.view: Right action is doing one's duty from the moral law
Right action is pursuing the good and flourishing

disputes.q: Do duties bind unconditionally, or depend on consequences?

sides.view: Categorical, exceptionless duties
Duties yield to the greater good

disputes.q: What is the source of duty?

sides.view: Reason's own law
God's command, or the social contract, or one's role

positions.name: Cicero
positions.claim: Our obligations flow from our nature and roles and the demands of honesty and the common good.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: To act from duty is to act from respect for the moral law; the categorical imperative binds unconditionally.

positions.name: The utilitarians
positions.claim: Our one duty is to promote the greatest happiness; particular duties are rules that serve it.

positions.name: Bradley
positions.claim: 'My station and its duties' -- obligation is concretely embodied in one's social roles.

key_texts.text: Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals

ideas.example: Kant insists the shopkeeper who is honest only because it's good for business acts rightly but without moral worth; duty done for duty's sake alone counts.
ideas.hook: What you owe, want it or not.

quotes.text: Act only on that maxim you can will to become a universal law.
quotes.context: The categorical imperative's first formulation. The test is not consequences but consistency: a maxim like lying to escape debt cannot be universalized, since it would destroy the practice of promising it depends on.

ideas.name: Education
ideas.gist: The forming of a human being—mind and character.
ideas.framing: Education is the forming of mind and character -- the passing on of knowledge, skill, and virtue to the young. What its ends should be, what should be taught, and who should control it are questions on which the future of every society turns.
senses: The cultivation of virtue and character (moral formation)
The transmission of knowledge and skill (instruction)
The drawing-out of the learner's own powers vs. filling with content
Liberal education vs. vocational training

disputes.q: What is education for -- virtue, knowledge, or use?

sides.view: The formation of virtuous citizens and souls
Useful knowledge and productive skill
The free development of the individual

disputes.q: Is learning discovery or transmission?

sides.view: Knowledge is recollected or drawn out from within
The mind is filled from without by instruction

disputes.q: Who should control education?

sides.view: The state must form its citizens
The family and individual, guarding against indoctrination

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Education turns the soul from shadows toward the good; the guardians undergo a long, ordered ascent to knowledge.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Education habituates the young to virtue and prepares them for the leisure of the free citizen.

positions.name: Rousseau
positions.claim: In Emile, education should follow nature, shielding the child's growth from corrupting society.

positions.name: Dewey
positions.claim: Education is growth through experience; the school is a form of community life -- learning by doing.

ideas.example: Plato's cave: education is not installing sight in blind eyes but turning the whole soul away from shadows toward the sun—a conversion, not a filling.
ideas.hook: Turning the soul toward the light.

quotes.text: The turning around of the soul.
quotes.context: Education does not put sight into blind eyes. The capacity to know is already there; teaching turns it away from shadows and toward what is real -- which is why it is compared to being dragged out of a cave.

ideas.name: Element
ideas.gist: The simplest constituents from which all else is composed.
ideas.framing: An element is a first, simplest constituent out of which composite things are made and into which they resolve. What counts as elementary -- earth, water, air, fire; atoms; or chemical simples -- marks each era's picture of matter.
senses: One of the classical four (or five) roots
The indivisible atom
A chemical simple (the modern sense)
Any basic constituent (of a proof, a language)

disputes.q: What are the true elements?

sides.view: Four roots: earth, water, air, fire
Indivisible atoms and the void

disputes.q: Is matter continuous or atomic?

sides.view: Matter is infinitely divisible; no smallest part
Matter is composed of indivisible atoms

disputes.q: Are elements changeable into one another?

sides.view: The elements transform into one another
Elements are permanent, distinct kinds

positions.name: Empedocles
positions.claim: Four roots combine and separate under the forces of Love and Strife.

positions.name: Democritus
positions.claim: Atoms differing in shape, order, and position, moving in the void, compose all things.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Four elements defined by pairs of qualities (hot/cold, wet/dry), plus aether for the heavens.

positions.name: Lavoisier
positions.claim: An element is a substance not decomposable by chemical means -- the modern definition.

key_texts.text: Aristotle, On Generation and Corruption; On the Heavens
Lucretius, On the Nature of Things

ideas.example: Democritus proposed that if you kept cutting a thing you'd reach uncuttable pieces—'atoms'—whose arrangements explain every visible quality.

quotes.text: Earth, air, fire, and water.
quotes.context: The four roots, mixed and separated by Love and Strife. It let Greek thought explain change without saying being comes from nothing -- the elements persist while their combinations shift.

quotes.text: Matter is conserved through chemical change.
quotes.context: Established by careful weighing before and after reactions. It killed phlogiston and made chemistry quantitative, replacing the four elements with substances defined by analysis.

ideas.name: Emotion
ideas.gist: The stirrings of the soul that color thought and move action.
ideas.framing: Emotion, or passion, is the soul's stirred response -- fear, anger, love, joy, grief -- felt in the body and moving us to act. Whether the passions are to be trusted, trained, or conquered has divided the moral traditions.
senses: Passion (something undergone) vs. action
A bodily-felt movement of appetite
An emotion involving judgment or belief (the cognitive view)
Emotion as distinct from reason and from calm desire

disputes.q: Are emotions judgments or brute feelings?

sides.view: They contain evaluative judgments
They are bodily feelings, even prior to thought

disputes.q: Should the passions be uprooted or moderated?

sides.view: Uproot them -- the sage is passionless
Moderate and habituate them to reason

disputes.q: Are emotions obstacles to reason or aids?

sides.view: They cloud judgment
Rightly trained, they are part of virtue

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Virtue is partly feeling the right emotions, to the right degree, at the right time.

positions.name: The Stoics
positions.claim: Passions are mistaken judgments about good and evil; the wise achieve freedom from them.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: Catalogues the passions as motions of the 'animal spirits,' to be mastered by the will.

positions.name: Spinoza
positions.claim: The emotions follow necessary laws; freedom comes through understanding them.

positions.name: William James
positions.claim: Emotion is the felt perception of bodily changes -- we are afraid because we tremble.

key_texts.text: Descartes, The Passions of the Soul

ideas.example: Spinoza held that an emotion 'ceases to be a passion as soon as we form a clear idea of it'—understanding your anger changes it.

quotes.text: We are afraid because we tremble.
quotes.context: The reversal of common sense. Emotion is the felt perception of bodily changes rather than their cause -- take away the racing heart and clenched stomach, James argues, and no emotion remains.

ideas.name: Eternity
ideas.gist: Timeless being—or endless time.
ideas.framing: Eternity is being without beginning, end, or succession -- either endless time or a timeless present. It frames how we conceive God, the soul, truth, and whether the world itself had a beginning.
senses: Endless duration (sempiternity)
Timelessness -- the whole possessed at once
The eternal as the necessary and unchanging (Forms, truths)
Eternity vs. the merely everlasting

disputes.q: Is eternity timeless or endless time?

sides.view: The complete, simultaneous possession of unlimited life -- timeless
Unending temporal duration
sides.who: much ordinary and some philosophical usage

disputes.q: Did the world have a beginning?

sides.view: The world is eternal, without temporal beginning
The world was created and began to be
Reason cannot decide the question

disputes.q: Is anything besides God eternal?

sides.view: Forms and mathematical truths are eternal
Only God is eternal; creatures are temporal or everlasting by gift

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: The Forms and truths of mathematics are eternal; time is 'a moving image of eternity.'

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Motion and the world are eternal; the prime mover is eternal actuality.

positions.name: Boethius
positions.claim: God's eternity is the whole of life possessed at once, reconciling foreknowledge and freedom.

positions.name: Augustine
positions.claim: God created time together with the world; there is no 'before' creation.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Whether the world is eternal or began is an antinomy reason cannot resolve.

topics: The eternity or beginning of the world
ideas.example: Boethius pictures God's eternity not as a very long time but as the total, simultaneous grasp of all life—no before or after, all present at once.
ideas.hook: All at once, no before or after.

quotes.text: Time is a moving image of eternity.
quotes.context: Made when describing the creation of the cosmos. Time is not a rival to eternity but its likeness: the everlasting order copied into a form that unfolds successively, because a made world cannot be eternal outright.

quotes.text: What was God doing before he made heaven and earth?
quotes.context: Augustine raises the objection to dismiss it: since God made time along with the world, there is no 'before' to ask about. The question assumes the very thing it disputes.

ideas.name: Evolution
ideas.gist: The descent and transformation of living kinds over time.
ideas.framing: Evolution is the idea that the forms of life -- and perhaps of all things -- develop and change over time rather than being fixed once for all. It transformed biology and challenged older beliefs in fixed species and design.
senses: The descent of species with modification (biological)
Any gradual development or unfolding (cosmic, social)
Evolution by natural selection (Darwin's mechanism)
Evolution vs. the fixity of species and special creation

disputes.q: Are species fixed or mutable?

sides.view: Each kind is fixed by its eternal form or by creation
Species descend and change over time

disputes.q: What drives evolution?

sides.view: Chance variation sifted by natural selection
The inheritance of acquired characteristics
A directing purpose or vital force

disputes.q: Does evolution abolish design and purpose?

sides.view: Yes -- apparent design is the work of blind selection
Evolution is the means of a larger providence

positions.name: Lamarck
positions.claim: Organisms change by use and disuse, passing acquired characteristics to their offspring.

positions.name: Darwin
positions.claim: Descent with modification through natural selection acting on chance variation.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: By contrast holds species eternal; nature acts for ends, not by cumulative accident.

positions.name: The modern synthesis
positions.claim: Heredity -- genes -- supplies the variation on which selection works.

topics: The origin of life and of man

key_texts.text: Darwin, On the Origin of Species; The Descent of Man

ideas.example: Darwin's finches: island by island their beaks differed to match available food, suggesting one ancestral kind had diverged rather than being separately created.

quotes.text: Descent with modification.
quotes.context: Darwin's own phrase for the theory; the word 'evolution' barely appears. He is careful to claim only that species change and share ancestry -- natural selection is the mechanism he proposes for how.

ideas.name: Experience
ideas.gist: What the senses and living deliver to the mind.
ideas.framing: Experience is what we learn through the senses and through living -- the encounter with particular facts. Whether experience is the source of all knowledge, or merely its occasion, splits empiricists from rationalists.
senses: Sense-experience (perception of particulars)
Accumulated practical familiarity (the experienced person)
The tribunal of science (observation and experiment)
All conscious life, in the widest sense

disputes.q: Is all knowledge from experience?

sides.view: Yes -- the mind begins a blank slate
No -- some knowledge is a priori

disputes.q: Does experience yield necessity and universality?

sides.view: No -- only 'so far, always'
The mind supplies the necessary forms that shape experience

disputes.q: Are the senses trustworthy?

sides.view: They are the basis of all science
They deceive; trust reason

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Knowledge begins in sense; from many memories comes experience, and from experience art and science.

positions.name: Locke
positions.claim: There are no innate ideas; all the materials of knowledge come from sensation and reflection.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: All ideas derive from impressions; experience gives matters of fact but never necessity.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Knowledge begins with experience but is not all derived from it; the mind's forms make experience possible.

positions.name: Dewey
positions.claim: Experience is the organism's active transaction with its environment, not passive reception.

topics: Experience as the source of knowledge

key_texts.text: Aristotle, Metaphysics I; Posterior Analytics II.19

ideas.example: Locke's blank slate: a child born knowing nothing, its ideas all traceable to sights, sounds, and inner sensations—no truths stamped in at birth.

quotes.text: Custom is the great guide of human life.
quotes.context: Following his argument that no reasoning justifies expecting the future to resemble the past. Habit, not logic, is what actually carries us -- a description of our situation rather than a solution to it.

ideas.name: Family
ideas.gist: The first community, prior to the state.
ideas.framing: The family is the primary community -- of husband and wife, parents and children -- the first association from which larger society grows. Its nature, authority, and relation to the state are debated from the household of the ancients to modern individualism.
senses: The household (including its economy and, anciently, its slaves)
The natural community of reproduction and rearing
The basic unit of society -- the state in miniature
The family as private sphere vs. as object of political concern

disputes.q: Is the family natural or conventional?

sides.view: A natural association, prior to the state
A conventional, variable arrangement, open to reshaping

disputes.q: Should the family be preserved or transcended?

sides.view: The family is the seedbed of affection and society
Abolish the private family among the guardians for unity

disputes.q: What authority governs within the family?

sides.view: Natural paternal or parental rule
An equal partnership; and it differs in kind from political rule

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: The household -- husband/wife, parent/child, master/slave -- is the natural first community; the state grows from it.

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: For the guardian class he abolishes the private family, so that none says 'mine' -- securing the city's unity.

positions.name: Locke
positions.claim: Distinguishes parental authority, temporary and for the child's good, from political power.

positions.name: Hegel
positions.claim: The family, grounded in love, is the first moment of ethical life, completed in civil society and the state.

topics: The nature and origin of the family
The community of women and children (Plato)
ideas.example: Plato shocked readers by proposing guardians hold wives and children in common, so no ruler would favor 'his own' over the city—dissolving the family for the state.

quotes.text: The community of women and children.
quotes.context: His most notorious proposal: the guardians hold no private families, so none can say 'mine' of a child or spouse. Aristotle objects that what is everyone's care becomes no one's.

ideas.name: Fate
ideas.gist: The appointed order that binds even the gods.
ideas.framing: Fate is the idea that events are fixed in advance by an order beyond human control -- by the stars, the gods, necessity, or divine decree. It presses the question whether anything is truly up to us.
senses: Cosmic necessity or destiny
Divine providence unfolding in time
The decree of the Fates or gods
Fatalism -- the view that deliberation changes nothing

disputes.q: Is everything fated?

sides.view: All is bound by fate and necessity
Some things are 'up to us'; not all is fated

disputes.q: Does fate destroy responsibility?

sides.view: If all is fated, praise and blame are empty (the 'lazy argument')
We remain responsible for our assent even under fate

disputes.q: Is fate the same as providence?

sides.view: Fate is providence as executed in the temporal order
Fate is blind necessity, opposed to a provident God

positions.name: The tragedians
positions.claim: The Fates and gods weave destinies mortals struggle against but cannot escape (Oedipus).

positions.name: The Stoics
positions.claim: Fate is the rational order of the cosmos; freedom is the wise assent to necessity.

positions.name: Epicurus
positions.claim: The atomic swerve frees us from the 'tyranny of fate.'

positions.name: Boethius
positions.claim: Providence is the divine plan; fate its unfolding in time; foreknowledge leaves freedom intact.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: God's providence governs all, yet works through contingent and free secondary causes.

topics: The meaning of fate and destiny
ideas.example: Oedipus does everything to avoid killing his father and marrying his mother—and each precaution is a step toward fulfilling exactly that fate.

quotes.text: An intelligence knowing all forces and positions.
quotes.context: The demon of determinism: for such an intellect nothing would be uncertain, and the future like the past would be present to its eyes. Probability, on this view, measures our ignorance rather than nature's looseness.

ideas.name: Form
ideas.gist: The shaping principle that makes a thing what it is.
ideas.framing: Form is what makes a thing the kind of thing it is -- its shape, structure, essence, or defining principle -- as opposed to the matter it informs. Whether forms exist apart from things, or only in them, is one of philosophy's oldest divides.
senses: Visible shape or figure
Essence or species (the what-it-is)
The Platonic Idea existing apart
The organizing principle of matter (substantial form)

disputes.q: Do forms exist apart from things?

sides.view: Forms are separate, eternal realities; things imitate them
Form exists only in the individual, joined to matter

disputes.q: Are universals (forms) real or names?

sides.view: Universals are real
Universals are mere names or concepts

disputes.q: Is form the intelligible in things?

sides.view: Form is the object of intellect; matter individuates
Only particulars are real; 'form' is our abstraction

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Forms are eternal originals; the soul knows them by recollection; particulars merely participate.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Form and matter are inseparable co-principles of substance; the soul is the form of the living body.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Substantial form gives a thing its being and species; God is pure form without matter.

positions.name: Ockham
positions.claim: Only individuals exist; universals are signs in the mind, not things.

key_texts.text: Aristotle, Metaphysics VII-VIII; On the Soul

ideas.example: The same bronze is a lump, then a horse, then melted and made a bell: matter persists, but form is what makes it, at each stage, this thing rather than that.
ideas.hook: What makes the stuff this thing.

quotes.text: The form is the essence and the primary substance.
quotes.context: His correction of Plato. Form is real and knowable, but it exists in things as their organizing structure rather than in a separate world -- what makes this flesh and bone a human being.

ideas.name: God
ideas.gist: The supreme being—ground of the world and its order.
ideas.framing: God is the idea of a supreme being -- creator, first cause, and highest good -- on which all else depends. Whether such a being exists, and what can be known of it, is perhaps the most consequential question in the whole tradition.
senses: The God of philosophy (first cause, unmoved mover, necessary being)
The God of religion (personal, providential, revealed)
The one God vs. the many gods
God as being itself vs. God as a supreme being

disputes.q: Can God's existence be proved?

sides.view: Yes -- by cosmological, design, and ontological arguments
No -- the proofs fail
God is known by faith, not proof

disputes.q: Is God's nature knowable?

sides.view: By analogy we affirm perfections of God
Only the negative way -- what God is not -- is safe

disputes.q: Is God personal and providential?

sides.view: A personal creator who knows and wills
God is the impersonal order of Nature itself

positions.name: Anselm
positions.claim: The ontological argument: that than which nothing greater can be conceived must exist.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: The Five Ways argue from motion, cause, contingency, degree, and design to God.

positions.name: Maimonides
positions.claim: We can say only what God is not; positive attributes mislead.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: Dismantles the design argument; the world's order does not prove a perfect designer.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Theoretical reason cannot prove God, but morality postulates him.

positions.name: Spinoza
positions.claim: God is the one infinite substance -- Nature itself -- not a person who chooses.

topics: Providence and the problem of evil
The one and the many gods
ideas.example: Aquinas's first way: things move only if moved by another, but the chain can't regress forever, so there must be a first, unmoved mover—which he calls God.
ideas.hook: The being all else depends on.

quotes.text: That than which nothing greater can be conceived.
quotes.context: Anselm's definition, not yet his argument. He then reasons that such a being must exist in reality, since existing is greater than being merely thought -- the ontological argument, disputed ever since.

quotes.text: The heart has its reasons which reason knows nothing of.
quotes.context: Not a licence for sentiment. Pascal means that first principles -- and the apprehension of God -- are grasped by an intuitive faculty rather than proved by demonstration.

ideas.name: Good and Evil
ideas.gist: The most basic distinction in the realm of action.
ideas.framing: The good is what all things seek -- the desirable, the perfective, the end of action; evil is its privation or opposite. What the good is, whether it is one or many, and how evil enters the world are founding questions of ethics and theodicy.
senses: The good as the object of desire and the end
The useful, the pleasant, the noble (kinds of good)
The highest good (summum bonum)
Moral vs. natural good and evil; evil as privation vs. as a positive force

disputes.q: Is the good one or many?

sides.view: A single Form of the Good above all
Good is said in as many ways as being -- no one Idea

disputes.q: Is the good objective or relative?

sides.view: A real feature of things, the end of nature
Whatever we desire or approve -- relative to us

disputes.q: Is evil real or a privation?

sides.view: Only the absence or corruption of a due good
A real, opposing principle

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: The Form of the Good is the highest reality, source of being and knowledge, like the sun.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: The good is that at which all things aim; the human good is activity of soul according to virtue.

positions.name: Augustine
positions.claim: All that exists is good insofar as it exists; evil is the privation or corruption of good.

positions.name: Hobbes
positions.claim: 'Good' and 'evil' are just names for what we desire and avoid; nothing is good in itself.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: The only thing good without qualification is a good will.

topics: The good as one or many
ideas.example: Augustine argued evil is not a thing God made but a hole in the good, as blindness is not a substance but the absence of sight—so no evil creator is needed.
ideas.hook: What to seek, what to shun.

quotes.text: Nothing in the world can possibly be conceived good without qualification except a good will.
quotes.context: Intelligence, courage and even happiness can be put to bad use; only the will that acts from duty is good in itself, whatever it manages to accomplish.

ideas.name: Government
ideas.gist: The organized power that rules a community.
ideas.framing: Government is the ruling power in a community -- the authority that makes and enforces its common decisions. Its origin, its forms, its proper ends, and the limits of its power are the enduring questions of political philosophy.
senses: The ruling authority, those who rule
A form or type (monarchy, aristocracy, democracy)
The activity of governing (administration)
Government vs. the state or society (the apparatus vs. the whole)

disputes.q: Whence does government derive its authority?

sides.view: From nature or God
From the consent of the governed -- a social contract

disputes.q: What is the best form of government?

sides.view: Rule of the best, or of one wise ruler
A mixed or balanced constitution
Representative democracy

disputes.q: What are the limits of government?

sides.view: It exists to secure rights and may be resisted if it violates them
Sovereignty must be near-absolute to keep the peace

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Distinguishes correct governments (for the common good) from perversions (for the rulers); prefers the mixed polity.

positions.name: Hobbes
positions.claim: To escape the war of all against all, men covenant to erect a sovereign whose power must be undivided.

positions.name: Locke
positions.claim: Government is a trust to protect life, liberty, and property; betraying it, it may be replaced.

positions.name: Montesquieu
positions.claim: Liberty depends on dividing and balancing the powers of government.

key_texts.text: Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws

ideas.example: Hobbes argued that without a common power to keep all in awe, life would be 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'—so we trade some liberty for order.

quotes.text: If men were angels, no government would be necessary.
quotes.context: Madison's case for checks and balances. Since neither rulers nor ruled are angels, the constitution must set ambition against ambition rather than rely on good intentions.

ideas.name: Habit
ideas.gist: The second nature built by repeated action.
ideas.framing: Habit is a stable disposition, acquired by repetition, that makes action easy, prompt, and reliable. It is the very stuff of character -- for virtues and vices alike are habits -- and the means by which we become what we repeatedly do.
senses: An acquired disposition or 'second nature'
Mere routine or custom vs. trained skill or virtue
Good habits (virtues) vs. bad habits (vices)
The learned automatic response (in psychology)

disputes.q: Is character made by habit or given by nature?

sides.view: We become just by doing just acts -- virtue is habituated
Temperament and nature set the limits

disputes.q: Is habit freeing or enslaving?

sides.view: It frees attention and perfects action
It deadens and mechanizes -- the enemy of thought

disputes.q: Can habit produce real virtue, or only its form?

sides.view: Repeated right action forms genuine virtue
True virtue needs right motive, not just habit

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Moral virtue comes about by habituation; we acquire the virtues by first exercising them.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Habits are stable qualities perfecting a power for good or ill; virtues and vices are habits.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: Custom is 'the great guide of human life,' the basis of causal expectation itself.

positions.name: William James
positions.claim: Habit is the great flywheel of society; make the nervous system an ally, not an enemy.

ideas.example: Aristotle: we aren't born just or brave but become so by practice, as a builder becomes a builder by building—character is habituated, not innate.

quotes.text: Habit is the enormous flywheel of society.
quotes.context: Habit keeps the social order running and saves us from deciding everything afresh. His practical advice follows: make the nervous system an ally rather than an enemy, since we are all bundles of habit by thirty.

ideas.name: Happiness
ideas.gist: The final end—what all else is sought for.
ideas.framing: Happiness is the good life fully lived -- the final end that all our actions aim at for its own sake. What it consists in -- pleasure, virtue, contemplation, or fortune -- is the central question of ethics.
senses: Flourishing, a life well lived (eudaimonia -- an activity, not a mood)
Pleasure or contentment (a subjective state)
Blessedness -- union with God
The greatest happiness (the utilitarian standard)

disputes.q: What does happiness consist in?

sides.view: Virtuous activity, crowned by contemplation
Pleasure, or freedom from pain
Virtue alone

disputes.q: Is happiness in our power or dependent on fortune?

sides.view: It needs some external goods and luck
It depends only on virtue, immune to fortune

disputes.q: Is happiness the right standard of morality?

sides.view: Yes -- the good is what conduces to happiness
No -- duty, not happiness, defines the moral

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Happiness is activity of soul in accordance with virtue, over a complete life, perfected in contemplation.

positions.name: Epicurus
positions.claim: Happiness is pleasure rightly understood -- freedom from bodily pain and mental disturbance.

positions.name: The Stoics
positions.claim: Happiness is virtue alone; nothing external is needed, for only the good will is truly good.

positions.name: Augustine
positions.claim: The heart is restless until it rests in God; true happiness is enjoyment of the eternal.

positions.name: Mill
positions.claim: The standard is the greatest happiness of the greatest number, higher pleasures counting for more.

topics: The contemplative vs. the active life
ideas.example: Aristotle warns we can't call anyone happy until we see how the whole life ends—Priam was fortunate for decades, then lost everything in old age.

quotes.text: One swallow does not make a summer.
quotes.context: Happiness is not a mood or a good day but an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue over a complete life -- which is why he says no one can be called happy until it is finished.

ideas.name: History
ideas.gist: The record and meaning of human events in time.
ideas.framing: History is both the course of human events and the inquiry that records and explains them. Whether history has a pattern or meaning, and whether it is science, art, or a guide to life, shapes how we understand our past and future.
senses: The events themselves (what happened) vs. the account or inquiry
Narrative and political history vs. the philosophy of history
History as a science of causes vs. an art of narration
History as unique and unrepeatable vs. as lawlike and recurring

disputes.q: Does history have a meaning or direction?

sides.view: It unfolds a rational or providential plan toward freedom
It is contingent, cyclical, or without overall meaning

disputes.q: Is history a science or an art?

sides.view: A rigorous inquiry into causes, even lawlike
An interpretive narrative of the singular

disputes.q: Does history teach lessons?

sides.view: It is philosophy teaching by examples
Its situations are too singular to yield laws

positions.name: Thucydides
positions.claim: Writes a rigorous, causal history 'as a possession for all time,' expecting patterns to recur.

positions.name: Augustine
positions.claim: History is the drama of two cities, moving under providence toward a divine end.

positions.name: Vico
positions.claim: History passes through recurring ages -- of gods, heroes, men -- knowable because men make it.

positions.name: Hegel
positions.claim: History is the rational progress of Spirit in the consciousness of freedom.

positions.name: Marx
positions.claim: History is driven by material conditions and class struggle toward a classless society.

topics: History as event and as inquiry
Progress, cycles, or providence in history

key_texts.text: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War

ideas.example: Tolstoy in War and Peace argues Napoleon merely rode a wave he didn't create; the war's course was the sum of countless small wills, not one man's plan.

quotes.text: A possession for all time.
quotes.context: His claim for the work's value against mere prize-winning performance. Since human nature stays constant, an accurate account of this war will be useful to anyone facing a similar crisis.

ideas.name: Honor
ideas.gist: The public recognition of worth—and the love of it.
ideas.framing: Honor is the recognition and esteem owed to excellence -- the outward reward of virtue and the mark of worth in others' eyes. Whether honor is a worthy aim or a snare of vanity has divided moralists and shaped the ethics of warrior and citizen.
senses: Public esteem or recognition (reputation, glory)
The inner sense of one's own worth (a code of honor)
The reward due to virtue
Rank or office

disputes.q: Is honor a worthy end?

sides.view: The greatest of external goods, the prize of virtue
A hollow, unstable good depending on others

disputes.q: Does virtue seek honor or scorn it?

sides.view: The great-souled man claims the honor he deserves
The sage is indifferent to reputation

disputes.q: Is honor rooted in others' opinion or one's own worth?

sides.view: It depends on the judgment of others
True honor is one's own conscience and integrity

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Honor is the greatest external good and the natural reward of virtue, but not the highest good itself.

positions.name: The Stoics
positions.claim: Honor and reputation are 'indifferents'; the wise care only for virtue.

positions.name: Hobbes
positions.claim: Honor is the acknowledgment of power; men compete endlessly for precedence and glory.

positions.name: Montesquieu
positions.claim: Honor -- the desire for distinction -- is the animating principle of monarchy.

key_texts.text: Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws

ideas.example: Falstaff asks what honor is—can it set a broken leg? 'A word.' Air.—deflating the battlefield glory his betters are willing to die for.

quotes.text: Honor is the prize of virtue.
quotes.context: The greatest of external goods, but still external -- which is why he denies it can be the highest good: it depends on those who bestow it rather than on the person honored.

ideas.name: Hypothesis
ideas.gist: The supposition put forward to be tested.
ideas.framing: A hypothesis is a supposition adopted to explain facts or to begin a line of reasoning -- provisional, to be tested or built upon. It marks the difference between what is assumed and what is proven.
senses: An assumption or postulate (in mathematics)
A tentative explanation to be tested (in science)
A conjecture whose consequences are examined
An unproven starting point ('from hypotheses')

disputes.q: Are hypotheses feigned or found?

sides.view: 'I frame no hypotheses' -- deduce laws from phenomena
Bold conjectures are indispensable to inquiry

disputes.q: Can a hypothesis be proved by its successful consequences?

sides.view: True consequences confirm it
Many false hypotheses also yield true consequences

disputes.q: Is scientific knowledge ever more than hypothesis?

sides.view: Theories can be true, not merely useful
All theory remains provisional

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: The mathematician reasons from hypotheses; dialectic rises above them to the first principle.

positions.name: Newton
positions.claim: Professes to 'frame no hypotheses,' deriving his laws from the phenomena themselves.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Distinguishes constitutive principles from regulative hypotheses that guide inquiry.

positions.name: Later methodologists
positions.claim: Science advances by proposing hypotheses and testing their observable consequences.

key_texts.text: Plato, Republic VI (the divided line); Meno
Kant, Critique of Pure Reason (Appendix to the Dialectic)

ideas.example: Newton described gravity's law precisely yet refused to guess its hidden cause—'hypotheses non fingo'—distinguishing a tested law from a mere conjecture.

quotes.text: Saving the appearances.
quotes.context: The task of devising geometrical models that reproduce observed motions. It leaves open whether the devices are real, which is why Copernicus could be read as merely calculating -- and why Galileo's realism was dangerous.

ideas.name: Idea
ideas.gist: The object of thought—concept, form, or mental content.
ideas.framing: An idea is an object of thought -- but is it a mental image in the individual mind, a concept, or an eternal reality independent of any mind? The word's history runs from Plato's eternal Forms to Locke's contents of consciousness.
senses: An eternal Form or archetype (Plato)
Any content of the mind -- perception, concept, image (Locke, Descartes)
Innate vs. acquired ideas
The exemplars in the divine mind

disputes.q: Are ideas in the mind or independent of it?

sides.view: Mental contents
Eternal, mind-independent Forms

disputes.q: Are any ideas innate?

sides.view: Yes -- some ideas are inborn
No -- all come from experience

disputes.q: Do we perceive things, or only our ideas of them?

sides.view: We directly know things
We know only our own ideas (the veil of perception)

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Ideas (Forms) are eternal, perfect originals that particulars imitate; the mind recollects them.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: Ideas are the modes of thought; some -- God, the self -- are innate, clear, and distinct.

positions.name: Locke
positions.claim: Every idea comes from sensation or reflection; the mind starts empty.

positions.name: Berkeley
positions.claim: Ideas are all that exist for the mind; to be is to be perceived.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: Ideas are the faint copies of vivid impressions.
