topics: Ideas as Forms vs. as mental contents
Ideas and things (the veil of perception)
ideas.example: Berkeley pressed Locke's premise to its edge: if all we ever have is ideas, we can't peek behind them to compare—so why assume matter behind them at all?
ideas.hook: What the mind holds before it.

quotes.text: The mind is white paper, void of all characters.
quotes.context: The rejection of innate ideas. Everything written on the mind comes from sensation or reflection -- a claim with political force, since it denies anyone is born to knowledge or authority others lack.

ideas.name: Immortality
ideas.gist: Survival of the soul beyond bodily death.
ideas.framing: Immortality is the idea that the soul, or the person, survives bodily death. It joins metaphysics -- is the soul the kind of thing that can persist? -- to ethics and religion, for it asks whether justice requires an afterlife.
senses: Immortality of the individual soul
Impersonal survival (absorption into intellect or world-soul)
Bodily resurrection vs. immortality of the soul alone
Symbolic immortality (in offspring, works, fame)

disputes.q: Is the soul naturally immortal?

sides.view: Yes -- being simple and akin to the eternal, it cannot perish
No -- the soul dissolves with the body

disputes.q: Is it the soul or the whole person that survives?

sides.view: The soul survives, freed from the body
The whole person is restored in the resurrection of the body

disputes.q: Can immortality be proved by reason?

sides.view: Yes -- by the soul's simplicity and its grasp of the Forms
No -- it is only a postulate of practical reason

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: The Phaedo argues the soul, simple and kin to the eternal Forms, cannot perish.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Only the active intellect may be deathless; the individual soul is the form of a perishable body.

positions.name: Lucretius
positions.claim: Soul is atoms that scatter at death, so 'death is nothing to us.'

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: The rational soul is subsistent and immortal, yet awaits the resurrection to be complete.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Immortality cannot be proved, but is postulated so virtue and happiness may finally accord.

topics: Resurrection vs. immortality of the soul

key_texts.text: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III

ideas.example: Kant argued we can't prove the soul immortal, but morality demands endless progress toward perfection—so we must postulate a life long enough to achieve it.
ideas.hook: The part of you that outlasts the body.

quotes.text: Death is nothing to us.
quotes.context: An argument, not bravado: while we exist death is absent, and when death is present we do not exist. Since all good and evil consist in sensation, there is no subject left for death to harm.

ideas.name: Induction
ideas.gist: Reasoning from particular cases to general truths.
ideas.framing: Induction is reasoning from particular cases to general conclusions -- the move from what we observe to laws we did not see. Its power built modern science; its justification remains philosophy's most stubborn problem.
senses: Generalization from instances
The intuitive grasp of a universal from particulars (epagoge)
Complete (enumerative) vs. incomplete induction
The experimental methods of induction (Mill)

disputes.q: Can induction be justified?

sides.view: It grounds all empirical science
No argument justifies inferring the unobserved from the observed

disputes.q: Is induction rational insight or mere habit?

sides.view: A grasp of the universal in the particular
Custom and expectation, not reasoning

disputes.q: Does science really proceed by induction?

sides.view: Yes -- generalize from gathered data
No -- it conjectures and tests, never simply induces

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Induction leads the mind from particulars to the universal, supplying the principles reason then uses.

positions.name: Bacon
positions.claim: True induction ascends gradually from gathered instances, using tables of presence and absence.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: No reasoning justifies the leap from past to future; induction rests on custom, not proof.

positions.name: Mill
positions.claim: Formulates canons -- agreement, difference, residues, concomitant variation -- to find causes.

key_texts.text: Mill, A System of Logic III

ideas.example: Hume's challenge: the sun has risen every day, but no argument proves it must rise tomorrow—our confidence is habit, not logic.
ideas.hook: From these cases to the rule.

quotes.text: So far, always.
quotes.context: The most experience can license. That the sun has risen daily gives no demonstrative ground that it must rise tomorrow; the inference relies on an assumed uniformity that experience cannot itself establish.

ideas.name: Infinity
ideas.gist: The unbounded—in number, magnitude, or being.
ideas.framing: The infinite is the boundless or unlimited -- in number, magnitude, time, or being. Long treated as a paradox to be tamed, it forces a choice: can the endless actually exist, or only be endlessly approached?
senses: Potential infinite (always more, never completed) vs. actual infinite (a completed whole)
The infinitely large vs. the infinitely small
The mathematical infinite vs. the metaphysical infinite (God)

disputes.q: Does an actual infinite exist?

sides.view: Only a potential infinite; no completed infinite in nature
Actual infinites are coherent and exist (in mathematics, in God)

disputes.q: Is the universe infinite?

sides.view: The cosmos is finite and bounded
The universe is infinite or unbounded

disputes.q: Can the infinite be measured or compared?

sides.view: An infinite cannot be traversed, so time had a beginning
Infinite sets have precise, comparable sizes

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Rejects the actual infinite; infinity exists only potentially, in division and addition.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: God alone is actually infinite; all created things are finite.

positions.name: Galileo
positions.claim: Notes paradoxes (as many squares as numbers), warning that infinity defies 'greater' and 'less.'

positions.name: Cantor
positions.claim: There are different, comparable sizes of infinity; the actual infinite is mathematically respectable.

topics: The infinite in magnitude and number
Infinity and the beginning of time
ideas.example: Cantor showed the infinity of all decimals is strictly larger than the infinity of counting numbers—some infinities dwarf others.

quotes.text: The actual infinite.
quotes.context: Aristotle had allowed only potential infinity -- a series always extendable, never complete. Cantor treated completed infinite sets as legitimate objects and proved some are larger than others, reversing two millennia of caution.

ideas.name: Judgment
ideas.gist: The act of affirming or denying—where truth is won or lost.
ideas.framing: Judgment is the act of mind that affirms or denies -- joining subject and predicate into something true or false. It is the unit of assertion, the seat of truth, and, in conduct, the exercise of practical wisdom in deciding.
senses: The mental act of affirming or denying (vs. simple apprehension)
The proposition, as the thing judged
The faculty of subsuming particulars under rules (Kant)
Practical judgment -- good sense in deciding

disputes.q: Where do truth and falsity reside?

sides.view: In the judgment, not in isolated concepts
Elsewhere -- in things, or in language

disputes.q: Is judgment a distinct faculty?

sides.view: A special power of subsuming cases under rules, which cannot itself be taught
Reducible to association of ideas

disputes.q: Are there synthetic a priori judgments?

sides.view: Yes -- and they make mathematics and science possible
No -- judgments are either analytic or empirical

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Truth and falsehood exist only in the combining and separating of judgment, not in isolated terms.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Distinguishes the intellect's simple apprehension from its second act, judgment (composing and dividing).

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Judgment subsumes particulars under universals; how synthetic a priori judgments are possible is his question.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: Our factual 'judgments' about cause are really habits of expectation.

key_texts.text: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason; Critique of Judgment

ideas.example: A doctor may know every rule of medicine yet still need judgment to see which rule this patient, with these symptoms, actually calls for.
ideas.hook: Where a thought becomes true or false.

quotes.text: Truth and falsehood belong to combination and separation.
quotes.context: Neither 'man' nor 'white' is true or false by itself; only joining or dividing them yields something that can be true. This locates truth in the judgment rather than in the concept.

ideas.name: Justice
ideas.gist: Giving each their due—the bond of communities.
ideas.framing: Justice is rendering to each his due -- the virtue of persons and the first virtue of societies. What each is owed, whether justice is natural or conventional, and whether it pays to be just are among the oldest and most consequential questions.
senses: Rendering to each his due (suum cuique)
General justice -- lawfulness and complete virtue toward others -- vs. particular justice
Fairness and equality: distributive (proportionate) and corrective (arithmetic)
The naturally right vs. the merely enacted (natural vs. legal justice)

disputes.q: Is justice natural or conventional?

sides.view: Grounded in the human good and natural law
The interest of the stronger, mere convention
It arises by covenant, out of the state of nature

disputes.q: Does it pay to be just?

sides.view: The just soul is healthy and happy; justice is its own reward
The ring of Gyges suggests we are just only for fear of being caught

disputes.q: What is the criterion of distribution?

sides.view: Proportion to merit
According to need
Benefit to the least advantaged

disputes.q: Can a law be unjust?

sides.view: An unjust law is no true law
Law is valid by enactment, whatever its content

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: In the Republic, justice is each part of soul and city doing its own proper work; the just are happier than the unjust.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Distinguishes general justice (lawfulness) from particular; divides the latter into distributive (by merit) and corrective.

positions.name: Thrasymachus
positions.claim: Justice is nothing but the advantage of the stronger -- the ruling party's interest encoded as law.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Justice is grounded in eternal law; a human law against it is a perversion, not binding in conscience.

positions.name: Hobbes
positions.claim: Before the covenant nothing is unjust; justice begins with the common power that enforces contracts.

positions.name: Rawls
positions.claim: Justice as fairness -- principles chosen behind a veil of ignorance, permitting inequality only to benefit the least advantaged.

topics: Justice as a virtue of soul and of society
The just and the unjust law

key_texts.text: Rawls, A Theory of Justice (a modern extension beyond the original set)

ideas.example: Rawls asks what rules you'd pick for society if you didn't know whether you'd be rich or poor in it—ignorance of your place forcing fairness.

quotes.text: Justice is nothing else than the advantage of the stronger.
quotes.context: The challenge the whole Republic answers. Justice, he argues, is a con: rulers make laws in their own interest and call obedience virtue. Plato must show the just life is better even when injustice pays.

quotes.text: Behind a veil of ignorance.
quotes.context: The thought experiment: choose society's basic rules without knowing your class, talents, race or beliefs. Self-interest then produces fairness, since you might turn out to be anyone.

ideas.name: Knowledge
ideas.gist: Justified grasp of what is true—as against mere opinion.
ideas.framing: Knowledge is the mind's grasp of what is true -- but what marks it off from mere belief, and how far it reaches, are the founding questions of epistemology. To know is more than to be right; it is to be right with justification and assurance.
senses: Justified true belief (vs. opinion and ignorance)
Scientific knowledge of causes vs. practical know-how
Knowledge by acquaintance vs. by description
A priori vs. empirical knowledge

disputes.q: What is the source of knowledge?

sides.view: Reason and innate ideas
Sense-experience

disputes.q: Is certain knowledge possible?

sides.view: Yes -- of first principles, the cogito, mathematics
No -- suspend judgment

disputes.q: What is the object of knowledge?

sides.view: The unchanging universal or Form
Particulars grasped through the senses

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Knowledge is of the eternal Forms, distinct from opinion about sensibles -- true belief 'with an account.'

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: To know scientifically is to know the cause -- why the thing cannot be otherwise -- reached from experience.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: Clear and distinct perception, starting from the cogito, yields an indubitable foundation.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: Limits knowledge to relations of ideas and matters of fact; causal 'knowledge' is only probable belief.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Knowledge needs both intuition and concept: thoughts without content are empty, intuitions without concepts blind.

ideas.example: Plato's Meno: a slave boy 'discovers' a geometry proof by answering questions, suggesting knowledge is recollected and grounded, not just true by luck.

quotes.text: True opinion tied down by an account.
quotes.context: Plato's answer to what separates knowledge from a lucky true guess. Right belief is unstable and can run away; knowledge is belief anchored by reasons for it.

ideas.name: Labor
ideas.gist: Human work—its dignity, its burden, its value.
ideas.framing: Labor is the toil by which human beings wrest their living from nature and transform the world. Long despised as servile, it was raised by the moderns to the source of value, of property, and even of human self-making.
senses: Toil or work (the effort of production)
The source of economic value (the labor theory)
A servile burden vs. dignified self-realization
Manual vs. intellectual labor

disputes.q: Is labor degrading or ennobling?

sides.view: Servile toil, unfit for the free, who need leisure
The dignity and very essence of man

disputes.q: Is labor the source of value?

sides.view: Value comes from the labor embodied in goods
Value comes from utility, scarcity, and demand

disputes.q: Does labor ground property?

sides.view: Mixing one's labor with nature makes it one's own
Property has other, conventional foundations

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Manual labor is servile and, ideally, left to others so citizens may have leisure for politics and thought.

positions.name: Locke
positions.claim: Labor is the origin of property -- what a man mixes his labor with becomes his own.

positions.name: Adam Smith
positions.claim: Labor is the real measure of value; the division of labor multiplies its power.

positions.name: Marx
positions.claim: Labor is man's essential activity, but under capitalism it is alienated -- the worker estranged from product and self.

topics: The nature and dignity of labor
Labor as the source of value

key_texts.text: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations
Marx, Capital; Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts

ideas.example: Adam Smith's pin factory: one worker alone makes a few pins a day, but ten dividing the steps make thousands—the division of labor multiplying output.
ideas.hook: Work that makes and remakes the world.

quotes.text: He hath mixed his labour with it.
quotes.context: The labor theory of property. What is held in common becomes private when someone works on it -- provided, Locke adds, enough and as good is left for others, a proviso later readers press hard.

ideas.name: Language
ideas.gist: The system of signs by which minds meet.
ideas.framing: Language is the system of signs by which we mean and communicate -- the medium of thought, society, and tradition. Its origin, its relation to reality and to thought, and whether its structure limits or enables us are enduring questions.
senses: A system of conventional signs (words)
Speech (the distinctively human power) vs. writing
The inner word (thought) vs. its outward expression
Natural language vs. formal or ideal languages

disputes.q: Is language natural or conventional?

sides.view: Words are conventional signs, by agreement
Names fit their objects by nature

disputes.q: Does language mirror reality or shape it?

sides.view: It names a pre-given reality or thought
Its structure shapes how we think and what we can say

disputes.q: Is thought possible without language?

sides.view: Thought precedes and could exist without words
Thought is bound up with, even constituted by, language

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: The Cratylus debates whether names are correct by nature or by convention, without fully deciding.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Spoken words are symbols of affections in the soul; they signify by convention, not by nature.

positions.name: Augustine
positions.claim: Reflects on how words are learned and how they point beyond themselves to things and to the inner teacher.

positions.name: Hobbes
positions.claim: Names are marks for memory and signs for communication; truth lies in their right ordering.

positions.name: Locke
positions.claim: Words stand for ideas in the speaker's mind; misused language is a chief source of error.

topics: The nature and origin of language

key_texts.text: Augustine, On the Teacher; Confessions I

ideas.example: In the Cratylus, one side says names fit their things by nature, the other that 'dog' could equally have been any sound we all agreed to use.

quotes.text: Words are the signs of ideas.
quotes.context: The doctrine that makes meaning private: a word stands for an idea in the speaker's mind. Locke draws the consequence that most disputes are verbal, arising from men using the same words for different ideas.

ideas.name: Law
ideas.gist: The rule of reason binding a community.
ideas.framing: Law is the rule of conduct laid down by authority for the common good -- binding a community and backed by force. What law is, where its authority comes from, and how it relates to justice and morality are the central questions of jurisprudence.
senses: An ordinance of reason for the common good, promulgated by authority (Aquinas)
The command of a sovereign backed by sanction (positivism)
The kinds of law -- eternal, natural, human, divine
Law vs. mere force or custom

disputes.q: What makes a law valid -- justice or enactment?

sides.view: A law contrary to natural justice is no true law
Law is valid if duly enacted, whatever its content

disputes.q: Is there a natural law above human law?

sides.view: Yes -- an unchanging law, knowable by reason, binding all
No -- all law is human posit or command

disputes.q: Must unjust laws be obeyed?

sides.view: Unjust laws do not bind in conscience
Even bad laws must be obeyed for the sake of order

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Law is 'reason free from passion'; the rule of law is preferable to the rule of any individual.

positions.name: Cicero
positions.claim: There is one eternal, natural law, the same for all, from which just human laws derive.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Law is an ordinance of reason for the common good; human law draws its force from the natural law.

positions.name: Hobbes
positions.claim: Law is the command of the sovereign; without a common power to enforce it, covenants are but words.

positions.name: Austin
positions.claim: Law is the command of the sovereign backed by sanction -- its existence is one thing, its merit another.

topics: The kinds of law (eternal, natural, human, divine)

key_texts.text: Aristotle, Politics III; Nicomachean Ethics V
Austin, The Province of Jurisprudence Determined

ideas.example: Aquinas holds a law that violates reason and the common good is 'no law but a corruption of law'—mere force wearing law's clothes.

quotes.text: An ordinance of reason for the common good.
quotes.context: Every word does work. Law must be reasonable (not mere will), aimed at the common rather than a private good, made by proper authority, and promulgated. A decree failing these is not law but violence.

quotes.text: Law is reason free from passion.
quotes.context: The case for the rule of law over the rule of men: even a good ruler is subject to anger and appetite, whereas a standing law is not -- though Aristotle grants law's generality can fail the particular case.

ideas.name: Liberty
ideas.gist: Freedom from constraint—and freedom for the good.
ideas.framing: Liberty is freedom -- the absence of constraint and the power of self-determination. What it is to be free, in the soul, in the state, and before the law, and how liberty is reconciled with authority and with others' freedom, are central to ethics and politics.
senses: Political liberty (freedom from arbitrary rule, under law)
Personal and civil liberty (rights and a protected private sphere)
'Negative' liberty (absence of interference) vs. 'positive' liberty (self-mastery)
Free will (the freedom of choice)

disputes.q: What is liberty -- non-interference or self-mastery?

sides.view: The absence of external restraint
Self-rule -- obedience to a law one gives oneself

disputes.q: Is liberty opposed to law, or secured by it?

sides.view: Every law is a restraint on liberty
Where there is no law there is no freedom -- law secures liberty

disputes.q: How far may liberty be limited?

sides.view: Only to prevent harm to others (the harm principle)
Society may also enforce morality and the common good

positions.name: Hobbes
positions.claim: Liberty is the absence of external impediments; subjects are free wherever the law is silent.

positions.name: Locke
positions.claim: Freedom is not license but life under a known law; where there is no law, there is no freedom.

positions.name: Rousseau
positions.claim: Civil liberty is obedience to the general will -- the law one prescribes to oneself; man is 'forced to be free.'

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Freedom is autonomy -- the will's self-legislation of the moral law.

positions.name: Mill
positions.claim: Over himself the individual is sovereign; liberty may be restrained only to prevent harm to others.

ideas.example: Mill's harm principle draws the line: your liberty to swing your fist ends where another's nose begins; society may restrain you only to prevent harm to others.
ideas.hook: Free from constraint, free for the good.

quotes.text: Forced to be free.
quotes.context: The tradition's most contested phrase. Rousseau means that compelling someone to obey a law he helped make frees him from personal domination -- critics have read it as licence for coercion in freedom's name.

quotes.text: Over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign.
quotes.context: The harm principle. Society may restrain us only to prevent harm to others -- his own good, physical or moral, is not sufficient warrant, however much others disapprove.

ideas.name: Life and Death
ideas.gist: The line between the living and the lifeless—and its crossing.
ideas.framing: Life is what distinguishes the living from the inert -- self-nourishing, growing, self-moving; death is its cessation. What life is, whether it is more than matter in motion, and what death means for the self are among the deepest human concerns.
senses: The activity of an organized, ensouled body (nutrition, growth, reproduction)
Biological life vs. the 'life' of mind or spirit
Death as the parting of soul and body vs. the breakdown of the organism
Mortality as the human condition

disputes.q: Is life reducible to matter and mechanism?

sides.view: Life needs a special vital principle or soul
Life is physico-chemical process

disputes.q: Is death the end of the self, or a passage?

sides.view: Death is annihilation -- 'nothing to us'
Death frees the immortal soul

disputes.q: Should death be feared?

sides.view: No -- it is either nothing or a good
It is the ultimate evil, to be resisted

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Life is the self-nutrition, growth, and decay of a naturally organized body; the soul is its principle.

positions.name: Epicurus
positions.claim: 'Death is nothing to us': where we are, death is not; where death is, we are not.

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: The philosopher practices dying -- the soul's release from the body to contemplate the Forms.

positions.name: Montaigne
positions.claim: 'To philosophize is to learn to die'; facing mortality frees us to live.

topics: The principle of life (soul or mechanism)

key_texts.text: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III

ideas.example: Montaigne kept death in view not to be morbid but to disarm it—'he who has learned how to die has unlearned how to be a slave.'
ideas.hook: The vital spark, and its going out.

quotes.text: To philosophize is to learn to die.
quotes.context: Borrowed from Cicero. Montaigne's version is practical: rehearsing mortality strips death of its strangeness and frees us to live without being ambushed by it.

ideas.name: Logic
ideas.gist: The science of valid inference.
ideas.framing: Logic is the study of the forms of valid reasoning -- of what follows from what, apart from particular content. It is at once an instrument of every science and a discipline debated as art, science, or the very laws of thought.
senses: The art or instrument of reasoning (the Organon)
Formal logic (validity by form: syllogism, inference)
The laws of thought (identity, non-contradiction, excluded middle)
Symbolic or mathematical logic

disputes.q: Is logic about thought or about being?

sides.view: The laws of correct thinking
The most general laws of reality itself

disputes.q: Is logic a science or only an instrument?

sides.view: A genuine science
Merely a tool serving the other sciences

disputes.q: Is the syllogism the whole of logic?

sides.view: The syllogism is essentially complete
Modern logic of relations and quantifiers vastly extends it

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Founds logic with the syllogism: from two premises a conclusion follows by form alone.

positions.name: The Stoics
positions.claim: Develop a logic of propositions and if-then inference, complementing Aristotle's.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Logic is the a priori science of the understanding's forms; adds a 'transcendental logic.'

positions.name: Frege and Russell
positions.claim: Recast logic in symbolic, mathematical form, capturing relations and generality.

topics: The subject and use of logic

key_texts.text: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason (Transcendental Logic)

ideas.example: Aristotle's syllogism: all men are mortal, Socrates is a man, therefore Socrates is mortal—the conclusion forced by form alone, whatever the terms.

quotes.text: Reason is nothing but reckoning.
quotes.context: Reasoning is adding and subtracting names and their consequences -- an early conception of thought as computation, three centuries before machines that could perform it.

ideas.name: Love
ideas.gist: The force that binds—desire, friendship, charity.
ideas.framing: Love is the movement of the soul toward what it finds good or beautiful, and the bond that unites persons. Ranging from bodily desire to friendship to the love of God, it is at once the deepest human experience and a cosmic principle.
senses: Eros -- desiring, passionate love, longing for beauty
Philia -- friendship, affection between equals
Agape or caritas -- self-giving, charitable love
Love of the good and of God; self-love

disputes.q: Is love desire for what one lacks, or gift of what one has?

sides.view: Eros as lack, longing for beauty
Agape as generous self-giving, willing the other's good

disputes.q: Is love selfish or selfless at root?

sides.view: All love is finally self-love or self-interest
Genuine love wills the good of the other for their own sake

disputes.q: Can love be commanded, or is it a passion beyond will?

sides.view: Charity is a commanded love, an act of will
Love is a passion that simply befalls us

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Eros is the soul's longing, ascending from beautiful bodies to Beauty itself -- the ladder of love.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Analyzes friendship -- of utility, pleasure, and virtue; the best is mutual love of the good.

positions.name: Augustine
positions.claim: Rightly ordered love (caritas) turns the soul to God; disordered love (cupiditas) to lesser goods.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: To love is to will the good of another; charity is the highest of the virtues.

positions.name: Freud
positions.claim: Love (libido) is rooted in the sexual drive, sublimated into higher aims.

topics: The kinds of love (eros, philia, agape)
ideas.example: Plato's ladder of love climbs from one beautiful body, to all bodies, to beautiful souls and laws, and finally to Beauty itself—desire schooled upward.

quotes.text: Our heart is restless until it rests in you.
quotes.context: The book's thesis in its first paragraph. Every desire is finally desire for God; the wandering recounted in the Confessions is love mistaking its object, not lacking one.

ideas.name: Man
ideas.gist: The rational animal—subject and object of every inquiry.
ideas.framing: Man is the being who asks what he is -- the 'rational animal,' the union of body and soul, the maker of tools, language, and cities. Every conception of human nature carries consequences for ethics, politics, and the meaning of life.
senses: Rational animal (defined by reason and speech)
Image of God (the theological view)
One animal among others (the naturalist view)
Maker, worker, and social-political being

disputes.q: What defines the human?

sides.view: Reason and speech
Tool-making and labor
The image of God

disputes.q: Is human nature fixed or made?

sides.view: A fixed nature or essence
Self-made through history and society

disputes.q: Is man good or corrupt by nature?

sides.view: Naturally social and good
Naturally at war and self-interested
Fallen and in need of grace

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Man is the rational animal and by nature a political animal, fulfilled only in the city.

positions.name: Pico della Mirandola
positions.claim: Man has no fixed nature; he is free to shape himself toward beast or angel.

positions.name: Hobbes
positions.claim: Man is matter in motion, driven by appetite; without a common power life is 'nasty, brutish, and short.'

positions.name: Pascal
positions.claim: Man is a paradox -- a thinking reed, wretched and great, suspended between beast and angel.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: The human being is a person, an end in himself, belonging to a kingdom of ends.

topics: The union of soul and body

key_texts.text: Pico, Oration on the Dignity of Man
Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals

ideas.example: Pascal: man is a reed, the weakest in nature, but a thinking reed—the universe can crush him, yet he knows it does, and it knows nothing.
ideas.hook: The animal that asks what it is.

quotes.text: Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.
quotes.context: His description of life without a common power, not of human nature as such. The bleakness is the argument for the sovereign: men are not beasts, but without enforcement their reasonable fear makes conflict rational.

quotes.text: Man is a thinking reed.
quotes.context: The universe can crush him without knowing it does; he dies knowing. Human greatness lies precisely in the awareness of human frailty.

ideas.name: Mathematics
ideas.gist: The science of number, magnitude, and pure form.
ideas.framing: Mathematics is the science of number, magnitude, and pattern -- the very model of certain, demonstrative knowledge. What its objects are, and why it applies so uncannily to the world, are enduring puzzles.
senses: The science of quantity (number and magnitude)
The study of abstract structure and form
Pure vs. applied mathematics
The language of nature

disputes.q: What are mathematical objects?

sides.view: Real, eternal entities the mind discovers
Abstractions from sensible things, or mental constructions
Mere marks and rules

disputes.q: Are mathematical truths a priori or empirical?

sides.view: A priori and necessary
Very general inductions from experience

disputes.q: Why does mathematics fit the world?

sides.view: Because nature itself is mathematical
Because we impose mathematical form on appearances

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Mathematics studies eternal objects and turns the soul from becoming toward being.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: The mathematician studies the quantitative aspects of things by abstraction, not separate entities.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: Makes mathematics the model of method and unites algebra with geometry.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Mathematical knowledge is synthetic a priori, grounded in the pure intuitions of space and time.

positions.name: Mill
positions.claim: Even mathematics rests on very general inductions from experience.

ideas.example: Euclid builds an entire geometry from five postulates, showing how vast, certain knowledge can grow from a handful of self-evident starting points.

quotes.text: There is no royal road to geometry.
quotes.context: Said to have been his reply to a king who wanted an easier path. Demonstration cannot be shortened by rank: the proof must be walked through by anyone who would know.

ideas.name: Matter
ideas.gist: The stuff underlying change and bodily existence.
ideas.framing: Matter is that out of which things are made and that which persists through their changes -- the stuff, substratum, or bodily principle of the world. Whether matter is all there is, or the lowest rung of a richer reality, divides materialists from their opponents.
senses: Physical stuff or body
The substratum of change
Prime matter (pure potentiality, formless)
Extension (Descartes) or mass-energy (physics)

disputes.q: Is matter all that exists?

sides.view: Only matter is real; mind is material too
Mind or spirit is irreducible to matter

disputes.q: What is matter's nature?

sides.view: Matter is extension in space
Matter is potentiality, actualized by form
'Matter' is only perceptions; no mind-independent stuff

disputes.q: Is matter continuous or atomic?

sides.view: Continuous and infinitely divisible
Composed of atoms in the void

positions.name: Lucretius
positions.claim: Nothing exists but atoms and void; even soul is made of fine atoms.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Matter is potentiality; prime matter has no form of its own but can take on all forms.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: Matter is res extensa, pure extension, wholly distinct from thinking substance.

positions.name: Hobbes
positions.claim: All that exists is body in motion; there is no incorporeal substance.

positions.name: Berkeley
positions.claim: To be is to be perceived; mind-independent 'matter' is an incoherent abstraction.

key_texts.text: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things

ideas.example: Aristotle's 'prime matter' is pure potential—no shape, size, or quality of its own—knowable only as the 'what' that takes on form.
ideas.hook: The stuff that takes on shape.

quotes.text: To be is to be perceived.
quotes.context: Not the claim that things vanish when unobserved -- Berkeley holds God perceives them continually. His target is the notion of matter existing wholly unperceived, which he argues is unintelligible.

ideas.name: Mechanics
ideas.gist: The science of motion and force.
ideas.framing: Mechanics is the science of motion and its causes -- of forces, bodies, and machines. As the first branch of physics to be fully mathematized, it became the model of exact science and the heart of the mechanical worldview.
senses: The science of machines (the lever and simple machines)
The general science of motion and force (statics, dynamics)
The mechanical philosophy -- all nature as matter in motion
Celestial vs. terrestrial mechanics

disputes.q: Can all of nature be explained mechanically?

sides.view: Yes -- everything is matter in motion, pushing and pulling
No -- life, mind, and ends resist mechanism

disputes.q: Is motion natural, or does it require a cause?

sides.view: Bodies seek their natural places; motion needs a mover
Bodies persist in motion by inertia unless forced

disputes.q: Is action at a distance intelligible?

sides.view: Gravity acts across empty space
Only contact and impulse are intelligible

positions.name: Archimedes
positions.claim: Founds statics -- the law of the lever and the principle of buoyancy.

positions.name: Galileo
positions.claim: Establishes the law of falling bodies and inertia, mathematizing terrestrial motion.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: Makes matter in motion, governed by impact and conserved motion, the key to all nature.

positions.name: Newton
positions.claim: Three laws of motion plus universal gravitation unify mechanics into one system.

key_texts.text: Archimedes, On the Equilibrium of Planes

ideas.example: Newton's insight: the same force pulling an apple down holds the Moon in orbit—terrestrial and celestial motion obey one law.

quotes.text: Give me a place to stand and I will move the earth.
quotes.context: His boast about the lever. The point is that mechanical advantage has no theoretical limit: any weight can be moved by any force, given enough length of arm.

ideas.name: Medicine
ideas.gist: The art and science of health and healing.
ideas.framing: Medicine is the art and science of health and healing -- of the body's balance, its diseases, and their cure. It raises questions of art versus science, of nature's role in healing, and of the physician's ethical duties.
senses: A practical art (techne) of healing
A science of the body and its causes
Preventive vs. curative medicine
Health as balance vs. as the absence of disease

disputes.q: Is medicine an art or a science?

sides.view: A conjectural practical art, judging particulars
A rigorous science of causes

disputes.q: Does the physician heal, or only assist nature?

sides.view: Nature is the true healer; the doctor removes obstacles
Active intervention masters disease

disputes.q: What is health?

sides.view: A balance of the body's humors or constituents
The proper functioning of parts; the absence of pathology

positions.name: Hippocrates
positions.claim: Disease has natural, not divine, causes; the physician aids nature and, first, does no harm.

positions.name: Galen
positions.claim: Systematizes the four humors, whose balance is health and imbalance disease.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: The body is a machine; medicine studies its mechanism in order to repair it.

positions.name: Claude Bernard
positions.claim: Founds experimental medicine, seeking the constancy of the body's internal environment.

key_texts.text: Hippocrates, Airs, Waters, Places; the Oath
Claude Bernard, Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine

ideas.example: Hippocrates broke with superstition by treating epilepsy, the 'sacred disease,' as having natural causes like any other illness—medicine as science, not magic.

quotes.text: First, do no harm.
quotes.context: The physician's restraint, following from the view that nature is the true healer. Since intervention can worsen what would have mended, the burden lies on the one who acts.

ideas.name: Memory and Imagination
ideas.gist: The powers that retain the past and picture the absent.
ideas.framing: Memory retains and recovers the past; imagination forms images of what is absent, past, or merely possible. Together they mediate between sense and thought -- the storehouse and the workshop of the mind.
senses: Memory as retention and recollection of the past
Imagination as image-making: reproductive (recombining) vs. productive (creating)
Imagination as the bridge between sense and intellect
Fancy vs. the shaping imagination

disputes.q: Is memory a passive trace or an active reconstruction?

sides.view: A stored impression or imprint
An active recollection that reconstructs

disputes.q: Is imagination merely reproductive or genuinely creative?

sides.view: It only recombines what sense supplied
It is productive and shaping

disputes.q: What is imagination's role in knowledge?

sides.view: Indispensable -- the soul never thinks without an image
A source of error to be disciplined

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Memory is of the past and belongs to the image-making power; the soul never thinks without a phantasm.

positions.name: Augustine
positions.claim: Marvels at the vast 'fields and palaces of memory' where the self and even God are sought.

positions.name: Hobbes
positions.claim: Imagination is 'decaying sense'; memory is sense remembered.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: Imagination freely combines ideas, but only from materials given by impressions.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: The productive imagination synthesizes the manifold, mediating intuition and concept.

key_texts.text: Aristotle, On Memory; On the Soul III

ideas.example: Augustine marvels at memory as vast fields and palaces where he meets himself and even recalls forgetting—an inner world larger than the outer.
ideas.hook: Holding the past, picturing the absent.

quotes.text: The fields and vast palaces of memory.
quotes.context: Augustine is astonished that the mind cannot contain itself: memory holds images, skills, emotions, even the idea of God, yet he cannot find where it keeps them or reach its limit.

ideas.name: Metaphysics
ideas.gist: First philosophy: the study of being as being.
ideas.framing: Metaphysics is the inquiry into the first principles and ultimate nature of reality -- being as such, substance, cause, God, and the categories every other science presupposes. Its very possibility as knowledge has been repeatedly affirmed and denied.
senses: The science of being as being (ontology)
'First philosophy' -- first causes and principles
The study of what lies beyond physics (God, soul, cosmos)
The a priori structure of thought (Kant's transformed sense)

disputes.q: Is metaphysics possible as a science?

sides.view: Yes -- the science of being and first causes
No -- it oversteps possible experience and breeds illusion
Only as a critique of reason's own limits

disputes.q: What is metaphysics about?

sides.view: Being as being, in general (ontology)
The supreme being, God (special metaphysics)

disputes.q: Are metaphysical statements meaningful?

sides.view: They state deep truths about reality
They are literally meaningless -- neither empirical nor logical

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: First philosophy studies being as being and its highest cause, the unmoved mover.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Metaphysics rises from creatures to God as being itself, distinguishing essence and existence.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: Reasoning beyond experience yields 'sophistry and illusion' -- commit it to the flames.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Old metaphysics is impossible as knowledge; a critical metaphysics maps the conditions of experience.

positions.name: Carnap
positions.claim: Metaphysical claims are pseudo-statements lacking any verifiable content.

key_texts.text: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason (Preface, Dialectic)

ideas.example: Kant compared past metaphysics to a battlefield of endless, undecidable combat—and set out to fix its borders so it would stop overreaching.

quotes.text: Commit it then to the flames: for it can contain nothing but sophistry and illusion.
quotes.context: The close of the Enquiry, on books containing neither mathematical demonstration nor experimental reasoning. The line became the slogan of later positivism.

ideas.name: Mind
ideas.gist: The thinking, knowing power—and its relation to body.
ideas.framing: Mind is the power of thinking, knowing, and willing -- the intellect that sets the human above the merely animal. Its nature, and its relation to the body, are among philosophy's hardest and most contested questions.
senses: Intellect or reason (the power of concepts and judgment)
Consciousness in general (all awareness)
The divine ordering Mind (nous)
Mind vs. brain (the mind-body question)

disputes.q: Is mind distinct from body?

sides.view: A distinct thinking substance
Identical with, or produced by, the body
The form of a living body

disputes.q: Is intellect separate from sense?

sides.view: Reason grasps universals beyond any sense
Thought is only refined sensation

disputes.q: Is there mind in nature or the cosmos?

sides.view: A world-ordering nous
Mind is only in animals and humans

positions.name: Anaxagoras
positions.claim: Mind (nous) is the ordering principle that sets the cosmos in motion.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: The intellect grasps universals; the active intellect may be separable and deathless.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: Mind is a thinking substance, better known than the body and really distinct from it.

positions.name: Hobbes
positions.claim: 'Mind' is nothing but motions in the body; all is matter in motion.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: The mind actively constitutes experience through its a priori forms and categories.

topics: The nature of mind and intellect
ideas.example: Descartes' cogito: even a deceiving demon can't make me doubt that I, doubting, exist—the one certainty from which mind rebuilds the world.

quotes.text: Thoughts without content are empty, intuitions without concepts are blind.
quotes.context: Kant's settlement of the rationalist-empiricist quarrel. Concepts without sensory input have nothing to be about; sensation without concepts cannot be organized into experience. Knowledge requires both.

ideas.name: Monarchy
ideas.gist: Rule by one—for good or ill.
ideas.framing: Monarchy is rule by one -- government in which sovereign power rests with a single person. From the philosopher-king to the absolute sovereign to the constitutional crown, it poses the question whether one ruler can best embody unity, wisdom, and order.
senses: Rule of one for the common good (the ideal) vs. tyranny (its perversion)
Kingship under law vs. absolute monarchy
Hereditary vs. elective monarchy
Constitutional or limited monarchy (the modern form)

disputes.q: Is rule by one the best form?

sides.view: One wise ruler gives unity and decisive rule
Concentrated power tends to tyranny; law and the many are safer

disputes.q: Should the monarch be above the law or under it?

sides.view: An absolute sovereign, source of law, above it
A king under the law -- else he is a tyrant

disputes.q: Whence the king's authority?

sides.view: By divine right or nature
By the consent or contract of the people

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: The ideal is the rule of the one who knows -- the philosopher-king, wiser than any law.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: True kingship rules for the common good and by law; lawless, it degenerates into tyranny.

positions.name: Hobbes
positions.claim: Favors an undivided sovereign -- most naturally one man -- whose absolute power alone secures peace.

positions.name: Locke
positions.claim: Rejects absolute monarchy, since none may rightly be judge in his own case.

positions.name: Montesquieu
positions.claim: In a moderate monarchy, intermediate powers and honor restrain the prince from despotism.

topics: Rule of one for the common good

key_texts.text: Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws

ideas.example: Aristotle's hinge: the king rules for the good of all, the tyrant for his own—same office, opposite aim, and that aim is the whole difference.

quotes.text: A king under the law.
quotes.context: The distinction between kingship and tyranny does not lie in the number of rulers but in whether power is bound by law and directed at the common good.

ideas.name: Nature
ideas.gist: The whole of things, and the essence of each.
ideas.framing: Nature means both the intrinsic principle that makes each thing behave as it does and the whole ordered system of such things -- the cosmos. It also sets a standard: what is 'according to nature' as against the artificial or the merely conventional.
senses: A thing's essence (its 'nature')
The inner principle of motion and rest
Nature as the totality of things (the universe)
The natural vs. the artificial, conventional, or supernatural

disputes.q: Is nature purposive?

sides.view: Nature does nothing in vain; it acts for ends
Nature is blind mechanism; ends are illusory

disputes.q: Is the natural the standard of right?

sides.view: There is a natural right or law above convention
Justice and law are conventional, not natural

disputes.q: Is nature identical with God?

sides.view: God and Nature are one (Deus sive Natura)
Nature is God's creation, distinct from Him

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Nature is an inner principle of motion and rest; each thing has an end proper to its kind.

positions.name: The Stoics
positions.claim: To live well is to live 'according to nature,' i.e., the reason pervading the cosmos.

positions.name: Spinoza
positions.claim: There is one substance, God-or-Nature; all things follow by necessity from its nature.

positions.name: Bacon
positions.claim: Nature is to be studied by its laws and, so understood, commanded for human benefit.

positions.name: Rousseau
positions.claim: Contrasts natural man -- good and free -- with man corrupted by society.

topics: The meaning of nature (essence vs. the whole)
The order and laws of nature

key_texts.text: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things

ideas.example: Aristotle distinguishes the natural from the made: a bed, if buried, would sprout wood not a bed, because its nature is the wood, and 'bed' is only art.
ideas.hook: The whole, and each thing's essence.

quotes.text: Live according to nature.
quotes.context: Nature here means the rational order of the whole, not raw impulse. Living according to it means accepting what is not up to us and exercising virtue in what is.

ideas.name: Necessity and Contingency
ideas.gist: What must be, and what merely happens to be.
ideas.framing: The necessary is what cannot be otherwise; the contingent is what can. Sorting the two runs through logic, nature, freedom, and theology -- deciding whether the world had to be as it is, or might have been different.
senses: Logical necessity vs. causal necessity
The necessary being (God) vs. contingent beings
Absolute vs. conditional (hypothetical) necessity
Necessity as compulsion vs. as unconditional certainty

disputes.q: Is everything necessary, or is there real contingency?

sides.view: All events are necessitated; contingency is only apparent
Some things are genuinely contingent, able to be otherwise

disputes.q: Is there a necessary being?

sides.view: Contingent beings require a necessary being as their ground
The inference to a necessary being is invalid

disputes.q: Are the laws of nature necessary?

sides.view: Nature's laws hold with necessity
They are contingent regularities that might have been otherwise

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Distinguishes the necessary, the possible, and the contingent; future contingents may lack settled truth.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: From beings that might not have existed he argues to a being that exists necessarily.

positions.name: Spinoza
positions.claim: Nothing is contingent; all follows with geometric necessity from God's nature.

positions.name: Leibniz
positions.claim: Separates necessary 'truths of reason' from contingent 'truths of fact,' grounded in God's choice of the best.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: No matter of fact is necessary; its contrary is always conceivable.

key_texts.text: Aristotle, On Interpretation IX; Metaphysics V
Aquinas, Summa Theologica I Q.2 (Third Way)

ideas.example: Aquinas's third way: contingent things need not exist, so if all were contingent, at some point nothing would have existed—hence something must exist necessarily.

quotes.text: Truths of reason and truths of fact.
quotes.context: The distinction later called necessary and contingent. Truths of reason are those whose opposite is impossible; truths of fact could have been otherwise, and rest on the principle of sufficient reason.

ideas.name: Oligarchy
ideas.gist: Rule by the few—typically the rich.
ideas.framing: Oligarchy is rule by the few -- typically the wealthy -- in their own interest. As the corrupt counterpart of aristocracy, it raises the perennial problem of the rich dominating the poor and of wealth translating into political power.
senses: Rule of the few (neutral) vs. rule of the wealthy few for themselves
Plutocracy (rule of the rich)
The perversion of aristocracy
The tendency of organizations toward rule by a few

disputes.q: Is oligarchy ever just?

sides.view: Rule of the few for the common good is aristocracy, not oligarchy
Property qualifications for rule are defensible

disputes.q: Is the root conflict wealth vs. poverty?

sides.view: The real political division is rich against poor, oligarchs against democrats
Other cleavages matter more

disputes.q: Can oligarchy be tempered?

sides.view: Mix it with democracy into a stable 'polity'
Concentrated wealth inevitably captures power

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Oligarchy arises when wealth becomes the qualification for rule; it splits the city into rich and poor.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Oligarchy is rule by the wealthy few for their own advantage -- the perversion of aristocracy.

positions.name: Polybius
positions.claim: Oligarchy is a stage in the cycle of constitutions, decaying from aristocracy toward mob rule.

positions.name: Michels
positions.claim: Even democratic organizations tend toward rule by a few -- the 'iron law of oligarchy.'

topics: The conflict of rich and poor
ideas.example: Aristotle's real dividing line isn't number but wealth: even if the rich were many and the poor few, rule in the rich's interest would still be oligarchy.

quotes.text: The iron law of oligarchy.
quotes.context: His conclusion from studying socialist parties committed to internal democracy. Organization itself breeds a specialized leadership that outlasts and outmaneuvers the membership -- who says organization says oligarchy.

ideas.name: One and Many
ideas.gist: How unity and plurality coexist in reality.
ideas.framing: How can reality be both one and many -- a single world yet countless distinct things? The tension between unity and plurality runs from the first cosmologies to disputes over identity, wholes, and the universal.
senses: The One as ultimate principle or source
Unity as a property of each being (a thing is 'one')
The many as a plurality of individuals
The universal (one) present in many

disputes.q: Is reality ultimately one or many?

sides.view: All is one; plurality is illusion
Reality is irreducibly many (atoms, monads, individuals)

disputes.q: How is the one present in the many?

sides.view: By participation in a single Form
By the same universal predicated of many

disputes.q: Is unity prior to plurality?

sides.view: The One is the first principle, source of all
Unity and plurality are correlative, neither prior

positions.name: Parmenides
positions.claim: What is, is one and continuous; division and change are unreal.

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Many sensible things are one by sharing a single Form; the Parmenides probes the puzzles.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: 'One' is said in many ways; the unity of a substance underlies its many accidents.

positions.name: Plotinus
positions.claim: From the ineffable One all multiplicity emanates and to it returns.

positions.name: Leibniz
positions.claim: Reality is a plurality of simple substances (monads), each mirroring the whole.

topics: The one and the many as first principles
Unity as a transcendental of being
ideas.example: Plato's 'one over many': many red things share one Form of redness—a single unity accounting for the scattered plurality we sense.

quotes.text: Entities are not to be multiplied beyond necessity.
quotes.context: The razor, in its traditional formulation. Ockham used the principle to cut away universals as real things existing apart from individuals, holding that only particulars exist.

ideas.name: Opinion
ideas.gist: Belief that falls short of knowledge.
ideas.framing: Opinion is belief that falls short of knowledge -- assent held without full certainty, which may be true or false. Ranking between ignorance and knowledge, it governs most of practical life and the whole realm of the probable.
senses: Belief without certainty (vs. knowledge)
Right opinion -- true belief lacking an account
The probable, in rhetoric and common life
Public opinion (a community's shared beliefs)

disputes.q: Is opinion sharply distinct from knowledge?

sides.view: Yes -- knowledge is of the stable Forms, opinion of shifting sensibles
They differ in degree of justification, not in kind

disputes.q: Can true opinion guide action as well as knowledge?

sides.view: Right opinion suffices for action, though it is unstable
Only secure knowledge is a safe guide

disputes.q: Should opinion be trusted or overcome?

sides.view: Reputable opinions are a proper starting point
Opinion must yield to reasoned knowledge

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Opinion lies between knowledge and ignorance; true opinion becomes knowledge only when tied down by an account.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Reputable opinions (endoxa) are the proper starting points of dialectical and ethical inquiry.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: Resolves to treat as false whatever is merely opinion, admitting only the certain.

positions.name: Locke
positions.claim: Where knowledge fails we must be governed by probability, proportioning assent to the evidence.

ideas.example: Plato notes that a true opinion about the road to a town gets you there as surely as knowledge—until, lacking grounds, it wanders off.

quotes.text: Opinion lies between knowledge and ignorance.
quotes.context: Not a middling amount of knowledge but a different object. Knowledge is of what fully is; ignorance of what is not; opinion of the world of becoming, which both is and is not.

ideas.name: Opposition
ideas.gist: The relation of contraries, contradictories, and correlatives.
ideas.framing: Opposition is the relation between things that stand against each other -- contraries, contradictories, correlatives. It underlies logic's laws, the analysis of change (between opposite states), and dialectics that make conflict the engine of thought.
senses: Contradiction (A and not-A)
Contrariety (hot/cold) and correlation (parent/child)
Privation (sight/blindness)
Logical opposition of propositions vs. real opposition of forces

disputes.q: Is the law of non-contradiction absolute?

sides.view: Nothing can both be and not be in the same respect -- the firmest principle
Reality contains real contradictions that drive its development

disputes.q: Do opposites explain nature?

sides.view: Change and nature are governed by pairs of contraries
Fundamental physics needs no contraries, only quantities and laws

disputes.q: Is opposition real or only conceptual?

sides.view: Some oppositions are real forces (strife, polarity)
Opposition is a relation among concepts and propositions

positions.name: Heraclitus
positions.claim: Opposites are one; strife is justice, and the world lives by tension.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Catalogues the kinds of opposition and defends non-contradiction as the ground of all reasoning.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Distinguishes logical opposition from 'real' opposition -- forces that cancel, like + and - quantities.

positions.name: Hegel
positions.claim: Contradiction is no mere error but the motor of dialectical development.

ideas.example: Aristotle sorts oppositions: hot/cold are contraries (a mean lies between), while being/not-being are contradictories (no middle is possible).
ideas.hook: Terms that stand against each other.

quotes.text: The same thing cannot at once belong and not belong to the same subject.
quotes.context: The principle of non-contradiction, which he calls the firmest of all. It cannot be proved without assuming it -- but he argues anyone denying it says nothing at all.

ideas.name: Philosophy
ideas.gist: The love of wisdom—reasoned inquiry into first things.
ideas.framing: Philosophy is the love and pursuit of wisdom -- rational inquiry into the ultimate nature of reality, knowledge, and the good life. Its scope, method, and very possibility as knowledge are themselves perennial philosophical questions.
senses: The pursuit of wisdom and the good life (a way of living)
The science of first principles and causes
The analysis of concepts and language (a modern turn)
Its parts: natural, moral, and first philosophy

disputes.q: Is philosophy a way of life or a body of doctrine?

sides.view: A transformative practice
A theoretical system or analysis

disputes.q: Can philosophy attain truth, or only clarify?

sides.view: It reaches first principles and the highest truths
It only analyzes or dissolves problems

disputes.q: What is philosophy's relation to science and faith?

sides.view: Their foundation
The handmaid of theology
An autonomous critical inquiry

positions.name: Socrates
positions.claim: Philosophy is the examined life; 'the unexamined life is not worth living.'

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: The philosopher ascends from the cave to knowledge of the Forms and should therefore rule.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: First philosophy studies being and its causes; the contemplative life is the highest happiness.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: Philosophy must be rebuilt from indubitable foundations, like a tree rooted in metaphysics.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Philosophy's task is critique -- to fix the powers and limits of reason itself.

topics: The value and limits of philosophy
ideas.example: Socrates chose death over abandoning inquiry, insisting 'the unexamined life is not worth living'—philosophy as a commitment, not a hobby.
ideas.hook: The love of wisdom, by argument.

quotes.text: The unexamined life is not worth living.
quotes.context: Spoken at his trial, refusing exile on condition of silence. Not a claim that philosophy is pleasant -- he is explaining why he would rather die than stop questioning.

ideas.name: Physics
ideas.gist: The science of nature—matter, motion, and energy.
ideas.framing: Physics is the science of nature -- of matter, motion, force, and the fundamental laws of the physical world. From Aristotle's study of change to the mathematical laws of the moderns, it is the arena where the deepest questions about reality become exact.
senses: The general science of nature (Aristotle's study of changing things)
The mathematical science of matter and motion (the modern sense)
Fundamental physics (ultimate constituents and laws) vs. its branches
Physics vs. metaphysics

disputes.q: Is physics qualitative or quantitative?

sides.view: A study of natures, qualities, and ends
The mathematical treatment of matter in motion

disputes.q: Are there final causes in physics?

sides.view: Nature acts for ends
Physics seeks only efficient causes and laws

disputes.q: Is nature continuous or atomic?

sides.view: A plenum of continuous matter
Atoms moving in the void

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Physics studies natural bodies as subject to motion and change, seeking all four kinds of cause.

positions.name: Galileo
positions.claim: Nature's book is written in mathematics; he reduces motion to measurable law.

positions.name: Newton
positions.claim: Formulates the laws of motion and gravitation, unifying the physics of heaven and earth.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: Builds a physics of extended matter and motion, banishing final causes.

topics: Force and the laws of motion
Final vs. efficient causes in nature

key_texts.text: (contrast) Lucretius, On the Nature of Things

ideas.example: Einstein showed that two events simultaneous for one observer aren't for another moving relative to them—time itself depends on the observer's motion.
ideas.hook: The laws of the material world.

quotes.text: I frame no hypotheses.
quotes.context: On the cause of gravity. He can state the law precisely without explaining what gravity is, and refuses to invent a mechanism -- a decisive shift from asking what things are to describing how they behave.

ideas.name: Pleasure and Pain
ideas.gist: The felt goads that drive us toward and away.
ideas.framing: Pleasure and pain are the most immediate goods and evils we feel -- the springs that draw us on and drive us back. Whether pleasure is the good itself, a sign of the good, or a distraction from it is one of ethics' oldest debates.
senses: Bodily pleasures and pains vs. pleasures of the mind
Pleasure as a feeling vs. as the unimpeded activity of a natural power (Aristotle)
Pleasure as the good (hedonism) vs. as a byproduct
The calculus of pleasures and pains

disputes.q: Is pleasure the good?

sides.view: Pleasure is the highest good and the end
The good life is virtuous activity, not pleasure

disputes.q: Are all pleasures equal, or higher and lower?

sides.view: Measure them only by quantity
Some pleasures are higher in kind

disputes.q: Is pleasure a process or an activity?

sides.view: The replenishing of a lack -- a process toward a state
The unimpeded activity itself, complete at each moment

positions.name: Epicurus
positions.claim: Pleasure is the beginning and end of the happy life -- but chiefly absence of pain and tranquility, not indulgence.

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Examines and limits pleasure's claim; unmixed pleasures rank below wisdom in the good life.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Pleasure is not the good but accompanies and completes good activity, as bloom crowns youth.

positions.name: Bentham
positions.claim: The good is the greatest pleasure; he proposes a calculus of intensity, duration, and the rest.

positions.name: Mill
positions.claim: Distinguishes higher from lower pleasures -- better Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.

topics: The nature of pleasure and pain

key_texts.text: Bentham, Principles of Morals and Legislation

ideas.example: Mill: better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied—some pleasures are higher, and those who've known both prefer them.
ideas.hook: The goads of gratification and distress.

quotes.text: Better Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.
quotes.context: His break with Bentham's arithmetic. Pleasures differ in kind, not just quantity, and the only competent judges are those who have experienced both.

ideas.name: Poetry
ideas.gist: Making in words—imitation, music, and vision.
ideas.framing: Poetry is imaginative making in words -- the art that, through image, rhythm, and story, moves and teaches. Its quarrel with philosophy over truth, and its power over the emotions, have made it a perennial subject of praise and suspicion.
senses: Imaginative literature generally (including drama and epic)
Verse or metrical composition
Poetry as imitation (of action, character) vs. as inspired vision
The old 'quarrel' of poetry and philosophy

disputes.q: Does poetry tell truth or falsehood?

sides.view: Poets imitate mere appearances and feed the passions
Poetry is more philosophical than history -- it shows the universal

disputes.q: Is the poet inspired or skilled?

sides.view: A divine madness seizes the poet
Poetry is an art with rules and craft

disputes.q: Should poetry please or instruct?

sides.view: Its end is delight
Its end is to instruct by delighting

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Banishes most poetry from the ideal city -- it imitates appearances and inflames the lower soul -- yet honors its power.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Defends poetry; tragedy imitates a serious action and, through pity and fear, accomplishes catharsis.

positions.name: Horace
positions.claim: The poet aims to profit and to please; art demands both talent and disciplined craft.

positions.name: Sidney
positions.claim: Poetry teaches virtue more movingly than philosophy or history, joining precept to example.

topics: The kinds of poetry (epic, tragic, lyric)
ideas.example: Aristotle defends poetry over history: history tells what Alcibiades did, but poetry shows what a person of a certain kind would do—the universal, not the mere fact.

quotes.text: Poetry is more philosophical than history.
quotes.context: History records what Alcibiades did; poetry shows what such a person would probably or necessarily do. By dealing in the universal rather than the particular, fiction can be truer than fact.

ideas.name: Principle
ideas.gist: A first thing—that from which something proceeds.
ideas.framing: A principle is a first thing -- a starting point from which something proceeds in being, in becoming, or in knowledge. Every science and every demonstration must begin from principles it does not itself prove.
senses: Principle of being (source of a thing's existence)
Principle of knowing (axiom, premise)
Principle of action (motive, rule)
First principles -- indemonstrable starting points

disputes.q: Are there indemonstrable first principles?

sides.view: Yes -- demonstration must rest on principles known without proof
All claims need justification; foundations are illusory

disputes.q: How are first principles known?

sides.view: By intellectual insight (nous) drawn from experience
They are innate to reason
They are habits or conventions, not intuitions

disputes.q: Is there one supreme principle of all?

sides.view: One first principle grounds everything (the One, God, the cogito)
Knowledge has many independent starting points

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Science demonstrates from first principles; the deepest, non-contradiction, is grasped by intellect.

positions.name: Euclid
positions.claim: Builds all of geometry from definitions, postulates, and common notions.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: Seeks one indubitable principle -- 'I think, therefore I am' -- as the foundation of knowledge.

positions.name: Leibniz
positions.claim: Adds the principle of sufficient reason: nothing is so without a reason why it is so.

topics: Principles of being vs. of knowledge
ideas.example: Aristotle argues demonstration can't go on forever; it must rest on first principles known directly—else nothing could ever be proved at all.
ideas.hook: The source the rest flows from.

quotes.text: I think, therefore I am.
quotes.context: The one thing that survives radical doubt: even a deceiving demon cannot make me not exist while I am being deceived. Descartes uses it as the fixed point from which to rebuild all knowledge.

ideas.name: Progress
ideas.gist: The idea that things improve over time.
ideas.framing: Progress is the idea that humanity advances over time -- in knowledge, in the mastery of nature, in morality or happiness. A hallmark of modern optimism, it is challenged by those who see cycles, decline, or mere change without betterment.
senses: Advance in knowledge and the arts and sciences (cumulative)
Moral and social progress (improvement of humanity)
History as a whole moving toward a better state
Progress vs. cyclical or declinist views of history

disputes.q: Does history progress, cycle, or decline?

sides.view: Humanity advances toward greater knowledge and freedom
History moves in cycles
Modernity is decline and corruption

disputes.q: Is there moral progress, or only technical?

sides.view: Mankind grows better as well as more knowledgeable
Knowledge and power grow, but virtue does not

disputes.q: Is progress inevitable or fragile?

sides.view: A law of history, all but guaranteed
Contingent, reversible, and easily lost

positions.name: Bacon
positions.claim: Knowledge advances cumulatively; the sciences will progressively extend human power over nature.

positions.name: Condorcet
positions.claim: Charts the indefinite perfectibility of the human mind and the onward march of enlightenment.

positions.name: Rousseau
positions.claim: Dissents -- the progress of the arts and sciences has corrupted morals, not improved them.

positions.name: Hegel
positions.claim: History is genuine progress -- the advancing self-realization of freedom.

positions.name: Comte
positions.claim: Humanity passes through theological, metaphysical, and positive stages toward maturity.

topics: Progress in the arts and sciences

key_texts.text: Condorcet, Sketch of the Progress of the Human Mind
Rousseau, Discourse on the Arts and Sciences

ideas.example: Rousseau's provocation: as the sciences and arts advanced, he argued, morals decayed—progress in knowledge is not automatically progress in virtue.
ideas.hook: The faith that things get better.

quotes.text: The indefinite perfectibility of the human mind.
quotes.context: Written while in hiding from the Terror that would kill him -- a fact that makes the book either the tradition's most heroic statement of hope or its sharpest irony.

ideas.name: Prophecy
ideas.gist: Speaking for the divine—foretelling and forth-telling.
ideas.framing: Prophecy is knowledge or speech that comes from God -- foretelling what is to come or declaring the divine will. It raises questions about revelation, about foreknowledge and freedom, and about telling true inspiration from false.
senses: Prediction of future events
The inspired declaration of God's word (not mainly prediction)
A mode of knowing (illumination of intellect and imagination)
The prophet as messenger and reformer

disputes.q: Is prophecy supernatural or a natural gift?

sides.view: A divine light elevating the mind
A perfection of imagination and virtue, not superior intellect

disputes.q: Can the future be foreknown without destroying freedom?

sides.view: Yes, through God's eternal vantage
Foreknowledge seems to fix the future

disputes.q: How is true prophecy told from false?

sides.view: By fulfillment and moral fruit
Private claims to revelation are politically dangerous

positions.name: Maimonides
positions.claim: Prophecy is a natural perfection of intellect and imagination, granted by God to the prepared.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Prophecy is a divine light raising the mind to judge and declare what surpasses natural reason.

positions.name: Spinoza
positions.claim: Prophets excelled in imagination and virtue, not speculative knowledge; prophecy adapts to its hearers.

positions.name: Hobbes
positions.claim: Warns that private claims to revelation threaten civil peace.

topics: Prophecy and freedom of the will

key_texts.text: Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed II

ideas.example: Maimonides made prophecy a natural summit: the prophet is one whose intellect and imagination are so perfected that divine truth can flow through them.

quotes.text: Prophets excelled in imagination, not in intellect.
quotes.context: A deflation with political purpose. If prophecy conveys moral certainty rather than speculative knowledge, scripture cannot settle questions of physics or metaphysics -- and clergy cannot claim authority over them.

ideas.name: Prudence
ideas.gist: Practical wisdom—knowing what to do here and now.
ideas.framing: Prudence is practical wisdom -- the virtue of deliberating well about what to do, and then doing it. It is the intellectual virtue that governs action, translating knowledge of the good into right choices amid particular, changing circumstances.
senses: Practical wisdom (phronesis -- right reason about action)
Foresight and good counsel
Everyday caution or self-interest (a narrower, lesser sense)
The charioteer of the virtues

disputes.q: Is prudence a virtue or a mere knack?

sides.view: A genuine intellectual virtue, uniting reason and right desire
Mere cleverness or cunning at getting what one wants

disputes.q: Can one be prudent without being good?

sides.view: No -- true prudence presupposes virtue and right ends
Yes -- one can deliberate shrewdly toward bad ends

disputes.q: Is prudence about means only, or ends too?

sides.view: It deliberates about means to ends set by virtue
It also perceives the right end in the situation

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Practical wisdom is right reason about things good and bad for man; it cannot exist without moral virtue.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Prudence is the charioteer of the virtues -- it applies universal moral principles to particular acts.

positions.name: The Stoics
positions.claim: Prudence is one face of the single virtue -- knowledge of what to choose and avoid.

positions.name: Machiavelli
positions.claim: Prudence becomes the ruler's shrewd calculation of means, adjusting to fortune and necessity.

ideas.example: Aristotle distinguishes the prudent person from the merely clever: cunning finds means to any end, prudence finds means to good ends—skill wedded to virtue.
ideas.hook: Knowing what to do, right now.

quotes.text: The charioteer of the virtues.
quotes.context: Prudence steers the others: courage and temperance supply right desire, but only prudence discerns what this situation actually requires. Hence one cannot be fully virtuous without it.

ideas.name: Punishment
ideas.gist: The deliberate infliction of hardship for wrongdoing.
ideas.framing: Punishment is the deliberate infliction of hardship on a wrongdoer by authority. What justifies it -- desert, deterrence, reform, or the restoration of order -- and what its limits are, lie at the heart of justice and law.
senses: Retribution (deserved requital)
Deterrence (preventing future crime)
Reform or rehabilitation (correcting the offender)
Protection of society (incapacitation); vs. mere revenge

disputes.q: What justifies punishment?

sides.view: Just desert -- the guilty deserve to suffer in proportion to their wrong
Its useful consequences -- deterrence, reform, protection

disputes.q: Is punishment about the past deed or the future good?

sides.view: Backward-looking: it answers to what was done (retribution)
Forward-looking: it aims at future benefit

disputes.q: Is capital punishment just?

sides.view: The murderer forfeits his life; justice demands it
It is cruel, ineffective, or not ours to inflict

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Punishment should heal the wrongdoer's soul, like medicine; no one does wrong willingly.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Punishment is a categorical demand of justice -- inflicted because the offender is guilty, in due proportion.

positions.name: Beccaria
positions.claim: Punishment is justified only to deter; it should be the least severe sufficient, and never capital.

positions.name: Bentham
positions.claim: All punishment is an evil, admitted only insofar as it prevents a greater evil.

positions.name: Hegel
positions.claim: Punishment honors the criminal as rational by annulling his wrong and restoring right.

key_texts.text: Bentham, Principles of Morals and Legislation
