ideas.example: Kant insisted even a society disbanding forever must execute its last murderer, lest justice be traded for utility—punishment as pure desert.

quotes.text: Punishment is an evil, admitted only to exclude a greater.
quotes.context: The utilitarian test. Since punishing inflicts suffering, it must be justified by the suffering it prevents -- which rules out punishment that is groundless, needless, or too costly to be worth it.

ideas.name: Quality
ideas.gist: The 'such' of a thing—its character, not its amount.
ideas.framing: Quality is the 'such' of a thing -- its character or way of being, as distinct from its quantity or relations. Whether qualities like color and warmth belong to things themselves or only to our perception reshaped the modern view of nature.
senses: Quality as a category (dispositions, capacities, affections, shape)
Primary qualities (size, shape, motion) vs. secondary qualities (color, sound, taste)
Intensive quality that admits of degrees

disputes.q: Do secondary qualities exist in things?

sides.view: Color, sound, and taste are really in the objects
Only primary qualities are in bodies; the rest are effects in us

disputes.q: Is quality reducible to quantity?

sides.view: All qualities reduce to quantitative arrangements of matter
Some qualities are irreducible features of being

disputes.q: Can qualities change by degrees?

sides.view: Qualities intensify and remit continuously (latitude of forms)
Qualitative change reduces to countable rearrangements

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Quality is a category; he distinguishes states, capacities, affective qualities, and figure.

positions.name: Galileo
positions.claim: Tastes, odors, and colors reside in consciousness; remove the living creature and they vanish.

positions.name: Locke
positions.claim: Primary qualities resemble their ideas; secondary qualities are powers to produce sensations in us.

positions.name: Berkeley
positions.claim: The primary/secondary distinction collapses -- all qualities are ideas in a mind.

topics: Occult qualities and the mechanical philosophy
ideas.example: Locke's split: a body's shape and motion (primary) are really in it, but its color and warmth (secondary) are powers to produce sensations in us.

quotes.text: Primary and secondary qualities.
quotes.context: Primary qualities -- size, shape, motion -- belong to bodies themselves; secondary ones like color and taste are powers to produce sensations in us. Berkeley replies that the same arguments dissolve both.

ideas.name: Quantity
ideas.gist: The 'how much' and 'how many' of things.
ideas.framing: Quantity is the 'how much' and 'how many' of things -- magnitude and multitude, the measurable aspect of reality. The rise of modern science was largely the decision to read nature in quantitative, mathematical terms.
senses: Continuous quantity (magnitude) vs. discrete quantity (number)
Quantity as a category of substance
Measure as the unit that makes quantity known
Extensive vs. intensive magnitude

disputes.q: Is nature fundamentally quantitative?

sides.view: The book of nature is written in mathematics
Qualities and ends are basic; mathematics abstracts from real nature

disputes.q: Is continuous quantity infinitely divisible?

sides.view: Magnitudes are infinitely divisible
There are indivisible minima or atoms

disputes.q: Is number real or a mental construction?

sides.view: Numbers are real, abstract objects
Number is a creation of counting minds and marks

positions.name: Euclid
positions.claim: With Archimedes, builds the exact science of magnitude and ratio.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Quantity is a category; number is discrete, magnitude continuous, and both admit of measure.

positions.name: Galileo
positions.claim: To know nature is to measure it -- to reduce phenomena to number, figure, and motion.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: Extension (quantity) is the essence of matter, making physics a kind of geometry in motion.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Quantity is a category; mathematics applies a priori to all appearances as extensive magnitudes.

key_texts.text: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason (Axioms of Intuition)

ideas.example: Galileo held nature's book is written in mathematics; Kelvin later pressed the creed—when you can't measure something, your knowledge is 'meagre.'

quotes.text: Number is the measure of multitude.
quotes.context: Quantity divides into the discrete, answering how many, and the continuous, answering how much. The distinction organizes arithmetic and geometry as separate sciences.

ideas.name: Reasoning
ideas.gist: The mind moving from what it knows to what follows.
ideas.framing: Reasoning is the movement of the mind from what it already knows to what follows -- inferring conclusions from premises. It is the discursive power that, unlike immediate insight, arrives at truth step by step.
senses: Inference (drawing conclusions from premises)
Deductive vs. inductive reasoning
Discursive (step by step) vs. intuitive (all at once)
Theoretical vs. practical reasoning

disputes.q: Is all reasoning reducible to the syllogism?

sides.view: Deduction is the core of inference
Induction and other forms are irreducible

disputes.q: Does reasoning discover truth or only unfold the premises?

sides.view: Deduction only draws out what is contained
Reasoning genuinely extends knowledge

disputes.q: Is reasoning distinctively human?

sides.view: Only rational animals reason
Animals infer, and machines compute

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Analyzes inference into the syllogism, distinguishing demonstrative, dialectical, and fallacious reasoning.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Reasoning (ratio) is discursive, proper to man; angels and God know by simple intuition (intellectus).

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: Sets rules for rightly conducting reason -- proceeding from simple, clear steps in due order.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: Distinguishes demonstrative reasoning (relations of ideas) from probable reasoning (matters of fact).

key_texts.text: Descartes, Rules for the Direction of the Mind

ideas.example: Hume's provocation: reason alone never moves us to act; it maps means to ends but the ends themselves come from passion—reason serves, it doesn't rule.

quotes.text: A syllogism is discourse in which certain things being stated, something else follows.
quotes.context: The definition founding formal logic. What matters is that the conclusion follows by necessity from the form alone, independent of what the terms are about.

ideas.name: Relation
ideas.gist: The being-toward that links one thing to another.
ideas.framing: A relation is a way one thing stands to another -- greater, cause, father, like. Long treated as the 'weakest' kind of being, relation became central to modern logic, physics, and the idea that things are constituted by their connections.
senses: Relation as a category (the 'toward something')
Real relations vs. relations of reason
Internal (essential) vs. external relations
Relation as the subject of relational logic

disputes.q: Do relations have real being?

sides.view: Relations are the least of beings, dependent on their terms
Relations are as real and basic as their terms; some are irreducible

disputes.q: Are relations internal or external?

sides.view: Relations are internal -- grounded in the natures of the related things
Many relations are external, not fixed by their terms' natures

disputes.q: Is space and time absolute or relational?

sides.view: They are real, absolute containers
They are systems of relations among things and events

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: The relative is what it is 'of' or 'than' another -- a distinct but dependent category.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Distinguishes real relations from relations of reason (as in the divine persons).

positions.name: Leibniz
positions.claim: Holds relations to be ideal; space and time are the orders of coexistence and succession.

positions.name: Russell
positions.claim: Relations are irreducible, objective, and the backbone of logic and mathematics.

topics: The relational theory of space and time
ideas.example: Being 'taller than' seems to add nothing to either person alone, yet it holds truly between them—prompting the question whether the relation is out there or in our comparing.
ideas.hook: The link between one thing and another.

quotes.text: The weakest kind of being.
quotes.context: Relations are real but dependent: fatherhood is nothing apart from father and son. Whether a relation adds anything to its terms became a central medieval dispute, sharpened by the Trinity.

ideas.name: Religion
ideas.gist: The binding of humanity to the divine.
ideas.framing: Religion is the bond between human beings and the divine -- expressed in belief, worship, and a way of life. It is examined as a source of truth, a social institution, a moral force, and, by its critics, an illusion.
senses: Worship and ritual (the cult)
A body of revealed belief (faith or creed)
Morality under a divine sanction
A natural human disposition or need

disputes.q: Is religion founded on truth or illusion?

sides.view: It rests on real knowledge of God
It is projection, wish, or 'the opium of the people'

disputes.q: Faith or reason -- which governs?

sides.view: Reason supports and clarifies faith
Faith stands above or against reason
Reason alone suffices (natural religion)

disputes.q: Is religion good or bad for society?

sides.view: It is the bond of morality and community
It breeds conflict and superstition

positions.name: Augustine
positions.claim: True religion is the soul's ordered love returning to God, its source and end.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Faith and reason are distinct but harmonious paths to the same God.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: Traces religion to fear and ignorance and criticizes miracles and the design argument.

positions.name: William James
positions.claim: Judges religion by its fruits in lived experience and defends the will to believe.

positions.name: Marx
positions.claim: Religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature, the opium of the people.

topics: The nature and origin of religion

key_texts.text: Hume, The Natural History of Religion
Kant, Religion within the Limits of Reason Alone
James, The Varieties of Religious Experience

ideas.example: Augustine's opening confession—'our heart is restless until it rests in Thee'—casts religion as the answer to a longing built into human nature.
ideas.hook: Binding the human to the divine.

quotes.text: The opium of the people.
quotes.work: Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right
quotes.context: Usually read as pure contempt, but the surrounding sentences call religion the sigh of the oppressed creature and the heart of a heartless world -- a painkiller for real suffering, whose cause is what Marx wants abolished.

ideas.name: Revolution
ideas.gist: The overturning of an established order.
ideas.framing: Revolution is the overthrow and radical remaking of a political order. Whether it is a crime against order, a right of an oppressed people, or the engine of historical progress divides those who prize stability from those who demand transformation.
senses: The violent change of government or constitution (political)
A fundamental transformation of the whole social order (the modern sense)
Revolution vs. rebellion or coup (systemic change vs. a change of rulers)
Revolution as a right vs. as a crime

disputes.q: Is there a right of revolution?

sides.view: A people may justly overthrow a government that violates its trust
Rebellion is never justified; it dissolves the order that makes rights possible

disputes.q: Is revolution progress or catastrophe?

sides.view: Revolutions drive history toward freedom and justice
They unleash chaos and tyranny, destroying accumulated wisdom

disputes.q: What causes revolutions?

sides.view: Inequality, injustice, and the desire for equality
Contradictions in the mode of production and class struggle

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Analyzes the causes of revolution (stasis) -- above all the desire for equality or superiority.

positions.name: Locke
positions.claim: When government breaks its trust, power reverts to the people, who may establish a new one.

positions.name: Burke
positions.claim: Condemns the abstract remaking of society; reform should respect prescription and grow organically.

positions.name: Marx
positions.claim: Revolution is the violent midwife of history, by which a rising class overturns outworn social relations.

key_texts.text: Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France

ideas.example: Locke grounded a right of revolution: when rulers break the trust and turn to arbitrary power, the people may reclaim the authority they lent.

quotes.text: A partnership between those living, those dead, and those yet to be born.
quotes.context: His counter to the revolutionary claim that each generation may remake society at will. The present holds society in trust, which is why he prefers reform that repairs to abstraction that rebuilds.

ideas.name: Rhetoric
ideas.gist: The art of persuasion by speech.
ideas.framing: Rhetoric is the art of persuasion -- of finding, in any case, the available means of moving an audience. Poised between philosophy and mere manipulation, it raises the question whether persuasion serves truth or supplants it.
senses: The art of persuasive speech
Eloquence, the art of speaking well
The three appeals (ethos, pathos, logos)
A neutral tool vs. flattery and manipulation

disputes.q: Is rhetoric an art or a knack?

sides.view: A genuine art, the counterpart of dialectic
Mere flattery, a knack for pleasing, not a true art

disputes.q: Does rhetoric serve truth or manipulate?

sides.view: Joined to knowledge and justice, it can serve truth
It persuades regardless of truth -- hence its danger

disputes.q: Is persuasion about reason or emotion?

sides.view: Argument (logos) is its body
Moving character (ethos) and passion (pathos) are decisive

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: In the Gorgias he condemns rhetoric as flattery; in the Phaedrus he allows a true rhetoric wedded to knowledge of souls.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Rhetoric is the faculty of discovering the available means of persuasion -- ethos, pathos, and logos.

positions.name: Cicero
positions.claim: The ideal orator unites wisdom with eloquence in the service of the commonwealth.

positions.name: Quintilian
positions.claim: Rhetoric is 'the good man skilled in speaking'; eloquence is inseparable from character.

topics: The means of persuasion (ethos, pathos, logos)
ideas.example: Aristotle's three levers: persuade by the argument (logos), by your credibility (ethos), and by the audience's feelings (pathos)—rarely by one alone.

quotes.text: The good man skilled in speaking.
quotes.context: His definition of the orator, answering Plato's charge that rhetoric is flattery. Eloquence divorced from character is not imperfect rhetoric but a different and dangerous thing.

ideas.name: Same and Other
ideas.gist: Identity and difference—the ground of all distinction.
ideas.framing: To think at all is to judge what is the same and what is different. Identity and difference underlie counting, classifying, personal identity over time, and the very logic of predication.
senses: Numerical identity (one and the same thing)
Specific or generic sameness (same kind)
Qualitative sameness (exact likeness) vs. otherness
Identity through time -- the 'same' self

disputes.q: What makes a thing the same over time?

sides.view: Same matter or bodily continuity
Same form or soul, or continuity of memory

disputes.q: Is the identity of indiscernibles true?

sides.view: No two things share all properties; total sameness is identity
Two distinct things could be exactly alike

disputes.q: Is personal identity substantial or constructed?

sides.view: A persisting soul or substance is the self
Identity is continuity of consciousness and memory
The self is a bundle of perceptions; no simple identity

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: The Sophist treats Same and Other as great kinds pervading all being.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Distinguishes numerical, specific, and generic sameness; difference within a genus defines species.

positions.name: Leibniz
positions.claim: The identity of indiscernibles: things differing in no property are one and the same.

positions.name: Locke
positions.claim: Personal identity is sameness of consciousness, not of substance.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: Finds no impression of a persisting self -- only a bundle in flux.

topics: Same and other as categories of thought
ideas.example: Leibniz claimed no two leaves are perfectly identical, for if they shared every property they'd be one thing—difference is guaranteed by distinctness.

quotes.text: The identity of indiscernibles.
quotes.context: If two things share every property they are not two but one. It follows from sufficient reason: God could have no ground for placing one rather than the other in a given position.

ideas.name: Science
ideas.gist: Organized, demonstrated knowledge of causes.
ideas.framing: Science is organized, demonstrative knowledge of things through their causes and principles. From Aristotle's certain knowledge of the necessary to the modern experimental enterprise, what counts as science has itself transformed.
senses: Certain knowledge of causes (Aristotle's episteme)
Any organized body of knowledge (a 'science' of X)
Modern natural science (empirical, experimental, mathematical)
The classification and hierarchy of the sciences

disputes.q: What makes knowledge scientific?

sides.view: Demonstration from necessary first principles
Testable prediction and experiment

disputes.q: Is science certain or provisional?

sides.view: It yields necessary truth
It offers ever-revisable hypotheses

disputes.q: Is there one method for all sciences?

sides.view: A single method (induction, or hypothesis-testing)
Different methods for different subject-matters

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Science is knowledge of the reasoned fact -- why a thing must be so -- demonstrated from first principles.

positions.name: Bacon
positions.claim: Calls for a new method: systematic observation and induction, to command nature by obeying it.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: Seeks a unified science on the model of mathematics, deduced from clear first principles.

positions.name: Newton
positions.claim: Unites experiment and mathematics, deducing universal laws from the phenomena.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Secures the a priori foundations that make natural science, with its necessary laws, possible.

ideas.example: Bacon urged replacing armchair deduction with active experiment—'twisting the lion's tail'—to force nature to reveal her causes.

quotes.text: Nature is commanded only by being obeyed.
quotes.context: The program of modern science in one line: power over nature comes not from magic or wishing but from discovering how nature actually works and conforming to it.

ideas.name: Sense
ideas.gist: The gateways through which the world enters the mind.
ideas.framing: Sense is the power of perceiving the world through the body -- sight, hearing, touch, and the rest. As the mind's first contact with reality, it is both the foundation of knowledge and, for its critics, a source of illusion.
senses: The external senses (sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch)
The 'common sense' that unites and judges them
Sensation vs. perception (bare feeling vs. perceiving an object)
Sense as the criterion of reality vs. sense as mere appearance

disputes.q: Do the senses give knowledge of things as they are?

sides.view: Yes -- perception is basically reliable
No -- they give only appearances and secondary qualities

disputes.q: Is all knowledge founded on sense?

sides.view: Nothing is in the intellect not first in sense
Reason has objects sense cannot reach

disputes.q: Are the sensible qualities in things or in us?

sides.view: In the objects themselves
Secondary qualities are effects in the perceiver

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Each sense receives the form of its object without the matter; the common sense integrates them.

positions.name: Democritus
positions.claim: 'By convention color, by convention sweet; in reality atoms and void' -- the senses report appearances.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: The senses often deceive, so they cannot be the foundation of certain knowledge.

positions.name: Locke
positions.claim: All ideas ultimately trace to sensation and reflection; experience furnishes the mind.

positions.name: Berkeley
positions.claim: Sensible things just are collections of ideas perceived; there is no unperceived sensible object.

key_texts.text: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things IV

ideas.example: Descartes noted a straight oar looks bent in water; since the senses sometimes deceive, he resolved to trust nothing they report without independent warrant.
ideas.hook: The world's gateways into the mind.

quotes.text: By convention sweet, by convention bitter; in reality atoms and void.
quotes.context: The first statement of the primary/secondary quality distinction. Colors and tastes are effects in the perceiver; what is really there has only size, shape and motion.

ideas.name: Sign and Symbol
ideas.gist: That which stands for something else to a mind.
ideas.framing: A sign is something that stands for something else -- pointing beyond itself to a thing, an idea, or another sign. The study of signs underlies language, logic, art, and religion, and asks how meaning is possible at all.
senses: Natural signs (smoke signifies fire) vs. conventional signs (words)
Sign vs. symbol (the arbitrary marker vs. the meaning-laden image)
The sign as pointing to a thing vs. to a concept
Symbols in religion, art, and mathematics

disputes.q: Are signs natural or conventional?

sides.view: Some signify by nature (symptoms), others by convention (words)
Which kind is basic remains disputed

disputes.q: Does a sign point to a thing or to an idea?

sides.view: Words signify things directly
Words signify concepts in the mind, which signify things

disputes.q: Is a symbol a mere substitute or does it share in its meaning?

sides.view: A conventional stand-in, replaceable at will
The symbol embodies and participates in what it means

positions.name: Augustine
positions.claim: A sign is a thing that, beyond its own appearance, brings something else to mind; distinguishes natural and given signs.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Sacraments are signs that both signify and, by God's institution, effect what they signify.

positions.name: Hobbes
positions.claim: Distinguishes marks (private aids to memory) from signs (public means of communication).

positions.name: Locke
positions.claim: Words are signs of ideas; meaning is the idea a word is made to stand for.

key_texts.text: Augustine, On Christian Doctrine II; On the Teacher

ideas.example: Augustine distinguishes natural signs, like smoke meaning fire, from given signs, like words—where a sound means only because a community agrees it does.

quotes.text: A sign brings something else to mind beyond itself.
quotes.context: The definition that founds Western semiotics. Augustine divides signs into natural (smoke of fire) and given (words), and treats interpretation as the central problem of reading scripture.

ideas.name: Sin
ideas.gist: The offense against the divine or moral order.
ideas.framing: Sin is moral evil conceived as an offense against God or the divine order -- more than mere wrongdoing, a rupture in one's relation to the highest good. It binds together ethics, freedom, and theology.
senses: Transgression of divine law
A disordered turning from God to lesser goods (privation)
Original sin (inherited fault) vs. actual sin
Mortal vs. venial sin

disputes.q: Is evil a positive thing or a privation?

sides.view: Evil is a privation of a due good, not a thing
Evil is a real, opposing principle

disputes.q: Is there original sin?

sides.view: Adam's fall corrupts the will of all his heirs
Each sins only by his own act; there is no inherited sin

disputes.q: Does sin require free will?

sides.view: Only the free can sin
Wrongdoing can be given a determinist account

positions.name: Augustine
positions.claim: Sin is the will's turning from the immutable good to mutable goods; original sin wounds all.

positions.name: Pelagius
positions.claim: Denies inherited sin; the will is free to keep the law, so grace is not strictly necessary.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Sin is an act against right reason and eternal law; he distinguishes mortal from venial.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Locates 'radical evil' in the free choice to set self-love above the moral law.

key_texts.text: Kant, Religion within the Limits of Reason Alone

ideas.example: Augustine's stolen pears haunt him because he stole not from need but for the thrill of the forbidden—evidence, to him, of a will drawn to evil for its own sake.
ideas.hook: Wrong as offense against the order.

quotes.text: Evil is the privation of good.
quotes.context: His escape from Manichaean dualism. Evil is not a rival substance created by God but a lack in something good -- as blindness is not a thing but the absence of sight.

ideas.name: Slavery
ideas.gist: The owning of persons as property.
ideas.framing: Slavery is the condition of one human being owned and ruled as the property of another. Defended in antiquity as natural and attacked in modernity as the deepest injustice, it forces the question of what is owed to every human being as such.
senses: Chattel slavery (the human being as property)
Slavery 'by nature' (the ancient defense) vs. by law or conquest
Political slavery (subjection to despotic rule)
Slavery as a metaphor for bondage to passion

disputes.q: Is any slavery natural or just?

sides.view: Some are slaves by nature, benefited by being ruled
All are born free and equal; slavery is always against nature

disputes.q: Is slavery merely conventional?

sides.view: It rests only on law, force, and convention, not nature
It reflects a real natural hierarchy

disputes.q: Can enslavement ever be legitimate?

sides.view: By just war or consent, to spare a life
No one can rightfully own another or alienate their freedom

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Holds some are 'slaves by nature,' lacking the capacity to rule themselves -- though many, he grants, are enslaved unjustly.

positions.name: The Stoics
positions.claim: All human beings share in reason; slavery binds only the body -- all are by nature free and kin.

positions.name: Rousseau
positions.claim: 'Man is born free'; to renounce liberty is to renounce one's humanity -- 'slavery' and 'right' contradict.

positions.name: Locke
positions.claim: Rejects voluntary self-enslavement, though he allows enslaving captives of a just war -- a much-criticized view.

topics: Slavery by nature vs. by convention
The ancient defense and its critics
ideas.example: Rousseau cut the old defense: might makes no right, for if force alone rules, then the moment the slave can break free, he does no wrong in doing so.

quotes.text: Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.
quotes.context: The opening line. Rousseau does not propose to strike off the chains but to ask what could make them legitimate -- his answer is a contract in which one obeys only rules one has authored.

ideas.name: Soul
ideas.gist: The principle of life—and perhaps of immortality.
ideas.framing: The soul is the principle of life and mind -- what makes a living thing alive and, in us, what thinks and chooses. Whether it is a separate substance, the body's form, or nothing beyond the body is a defining question.
senses: Principle of life (nutrition, growth) shared by all that lives
Seat of sensation and desire (in animals)
Rational intellect (in humans)
A separable substance vs. the body's form

disputes.q: What is the soul's relation to the body?

sides.view: A separate substance lodged in the body
The form or first actuality of a living body
Nothing but the body's functions

disputes.q: Is the soul immortal?

sides.view: Yes -- being simple and rational
No -- it perishes with the body

disputes.q: Do plants and animals have souls?

sides.view: Yes -- graded vegetative, sensitive, and rational souls
No -- animals are mere machines

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: The soul is immortal and tripartite -- reason, spirit, appetite -- ruling the body from within.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: The soul is the form or first actuality of a living body; its powers are graded.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: The soul is a thinking substance, wholly distinct from the extended body it inhabits.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: The rational soul is the single substantial form of the human being, subsistent and immortal.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: Finds no soul-substance -- only a bundle of perceptions.

topics: The parts or powers of the soul
The vegetative, sensitive, and rational soul
ideas.example: Aristotle rejects Plato's separable soul: as sight is to the eye, soul is to the body—the form that makes this matter a living thing, not a ghost within it.

quotes.text: The soul is the first actuality of a natural body having life potentially.
quotes.context: Deliberately deflationary. The soul is not a passenger in the body but the organizing form that makes it a living thing at all -- as sight is to the eye.

ideas.name: Space
ideas.gist: The extension in which bodies exist and move.
ideas.framing: Space is the extension in which bodies are located and move -- but is it a real thing, a mere relation among bodies, or a form our minds impose? The answer shapes physics and metaphysics alike.
senses: Place (the boundary containing a body) vs. space (extension in general)
The void or empty space
Absolute space (a fixed container) vs. relational space
Space as a form of intuition (Kant)

disputes.q: Is there void or empty space?

sides.view: A void is impossible; nature abhors a vacuum
Empty space exists and is needed for motion

disputes.q: Is space absolute or relational?

sides.view: Absolute space exists independent of bodies
Space is only the order of relations among bodies

disputes.q: Is space real or mind-dependent?

sides.view: Space is a real feature of the world
Space is the a priori form of outer intuition

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Denies the void and defines place as the inner surface of the containing body.

positions.name: Descartes
positions.claim: Identifies space with extended matter; there is no empty extension.

positions.name: Newton
positions.claim: Absolute space exists -- uniform, immovable, the frame of true motion.

positions.name: Leibniz
positions.claim: Space is nothing but the order of coexisting things; absolute space is a fiction.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Space is not a thing but the form under which we must perceive outer objects.

topics: Space as a form of intuition

key_texts.text: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason (Transcendental Aesthetic)

ideas.example: Leibniz argued that if space were an absolute container, God could have no reason to place the whole universe here rather than three feet over—so space must be relational.

quotes.text: Space is not an empirical concept drawn from outer experience.
quotes.context: We cannot derive space from experience because we must already presuppose it to have any outer experience at all. Kant concludes it is a form the mind contributes, not a property of things in themselves.

ideas.name: State
ideas.gist: The sovereign political community.
ideas.framing: The state is the sovereign political community -- the highest and most complete association, claiming authority over all within its bounds. Its origin, its ends, its rights over the individual, and its relation to society are foundational political questions.
senses: The political community or city (Aristotle's complete association)
The sovereign apparatus of authority (the modern state, monopolizing legitimate force)
The state vs. society (the political order vs. the broader social life)
The state as an end in itself vs. an instrument for individual ends

disputes.q: Is the state natural or artificial?

sides.view: Natural -- man is a political animal, completed in the state
Artificial -- erected by contract to escape the state of nature

disputes.q: Is the state prior to the individual, or the reverse?

sides.view: The whole is prior; the individual is fulfilled only in it
Individuals with rights are prior; the state serves them

disputes.q: What are the ends and limits of the state?

sides.view: To secure the good life and virtue
To secure peace and rights, leaving the rest free

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: The state exists by nature and is prior to the individual; it comes to be for life, but exists for the good life.

positions.name: Hobbes
positions.claim: The state ('Leviathan') is an artificial person created by covenant, ending the war of all against all.

positions.name: Locke
positions.claim: The state is instituted by consent to protect natural rights; its power is limited and held in trust.

positions.name: Rousseau
positions.claim: The state embodies the general will, through which a people becomes a sovereign moral body.

positions.name: Hegel
positions.claim: The state is the actuality of ethical life -- the realization of concrete freedom, higher than family or civil society.

topics: The nature and origin of the state
The state as natural or conventional
The state and the good life
ideas.example: Aristotle held the state comes to be for survival but exists for the good life—its point is not mere living together but living well.

quotes.text: Man is by nature a political animal.
quotes.context: Not that men are sociable, but that the human being is only completed in the polis. Speech exists to declare the just and unjust; one who needs no city is a beast or a god.

ideas.name: Temperance
ideas.gist: Self-mastery over pleasure and appetite.
ideas.framing: Temperance is the virtue that moderates desire and pleasure -- self-mastery over the appetites for food, drink, and sex. The discipline by which reason governs the body's cravings, it is a cardinal virtue and the mark of a well-ordered soul.
senses: Moderation of bodily appetites and pleasures
Self-control or self-mastery generally
The harmony of the soul's parts (reason ruling appetite)
The mean between self-indulgence and insensibility

disputes.q: Is temperance the same as self-control, or higher?

sides.view: The temperate person has ordered desires and feels no inner conflict
The merely continent must fight their appetites

disputes.q: Should appetite be moderated or denied?

sides.view: Moderate and order the appetites
Renounce and mortify them

disputes.q: Is temperance chiefly personal or also political?

sides.view: A virtue of the individual soul
Also the civic harmony where each part accepts its place

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Temperance is the harmony in which reason rules and appetite consents -- in soul and city alike.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Temperance is the mean concerning bodily pleasures; the temperate person desires rightly, not merely resists.

positions.name: The Stoics
positions.claim: Temperance is knowledge of what to choose in matters of desire; the sage is master of appetite.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Temperance restrains the concupiscible appetite according to reason; its parts include humility and chastity.

ideas.example: Plato locates temperance not in one part of the soul but in the agreement of all three about who should rule—harmony, not mere suppression of appetite.

quotes.text: The temperate man does not even desire wrongly.
quotes.context: His distinction between temperance and mere self-control. The merely continent resist temptation and win; the temperate have trained desire itself, so the struggle no longer arises.

ideas.name: Theology
ideas.gist: Reasoned discourse about God.
ideas.framing: Theology is reasoned discourse about God -- founded either on revelation (sacred theology) or on unaided reason (natural theology). Its scope and method mark the boundary, and the meeting-point, of faith and philosophy.
senses: Natural theology (God known by reason from creatures)
Sacred or revealed theology (from Scripture)
Theology as a science ordered from principles
The negative (apophatic) and mystical ways

disputes.q: Is theology a science?

sides.view: Yes -- it reasons from revealed principles
No -- it lacks self-evident premises

disputes.q: How much of God can reason reach?

sides.view: Much -- his existence and some attributes
Little or nothing without revelation

disputes.q: Faith seeking understanding, or reason grounding faith?

sides.view: Believe in order to understand
Reason must first secure its ground

positions.name: Augustine
positions.claim: 'Faith seeking understanding' -- belief first, then reason illumines what is believed.

positions.name: Anselm
positions.claim: 'I believe in order that I may understand'; reason unfolds the content of faith.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Sacred doctrine is a science drawing its principles from God's revelation; reason serves faith.

positions.name: Maimonides
positions.claim: Guards God's transcendence; negative attributes protect against anthropomorphism.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Speculative theology overreaches; God is a matter of practical faith, not theoretical science.

topics: The methods of theology (affirmation, negation, analogy)

key_texts.text: Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion

ideas.example: Aquinas treats theology as a genuine science that borrows its first principles from God's own knowledge, as optics borrows from geometry—faith supplying what reason cannot reach.

quotes.text: I believe in order that I may understand.
quotes.context: Reverses the modern order. Faith is not the conclusion of the argument but the condition of seeing it -- understanding deepens what is already believed rather than establishing it from outside.

ideas.name: Time
ideas.gist: The measure of change—past, present, and future.
ideas.framing: Time is the measure of change, the order of before and after -- yet what it is, and whether it is real, remains among the deepest puzzles. It binds together motion, memory, eternity, and the self.
senses: The measure or number of motion
Duration lived and felt
Absolute time (flowing uniformly) vs. relative time
The tensed present vs. the tenseless order of events

disputes.q: Is time real or ideal?

sides.view: Time is a real feature of motion and the world
Time depends on the numbering soul, or is a form of intuition

disputes.q: Is time absolute or relative?

sides.view: Absolute time flows equably, independent of all else
Time is an order of events, relative to observers

disputes.q: Does time have a beginning?

sides.view: Time began with creation; there was no time before the world
Time is eternal, without beginning

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Time is the number of motion with respect to before and after; he puzzles over the reality of past and future.

positions.name: Augustine
positions.claim: We measure past and future only in the present mind -- memory and expectation.

positions.name: Newton
positions.claim: Absolute, true, mathematical time flows uniformly without relation to anything external.

positions.name: Leibniz
positions.claim: Time is the order of succession, not a self-standing thing.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Time is the a priori form of inner sense, ordering all our experience.

topics: The reality of past and future
ideas.example: Augustine's famous confession: 'What then is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I wish to explain, I do not know'—the most familiar thing turned mysterious.
ideas.hook: The measure of before and after.

quotes.text: What then is time? If no one asks me, I know.
quotes.context: The most quoted line on the subject. Augustine's puzzle is that past and future do not exist and the present has no duration -- leading him to locate time in the soul's own extension.

ideas.name: Truth
ideas.gist: The agreement of thought with what is.
ideas.framing: Truth is the agreement of thought or statement with reality -- the goal of all inquiry and the standard by which belief is judged. What truth consists in, and whether we can attain it, are questions as old as philosophy.
senses: Correspondence (thought matching reality)
Coherence (fitting a consistent system)
What works (pragmatism)
Logical truth of propositions vs. the intelligibility of being; eternal vs. changing truth

disputes.q: What does truth consist in?

sides.view: Correspondence of statement to fact
Coherence within a system
Practical success

disputes.q: Is truth absolute or relative?

sides.view: Some truths are timeless and universal
'Man is the measure' -- truth is relative to the perceiver

disputes.q: Can truth be attained with certainty?

sides.view: Yes -- of first principles and clear ideas
The skeptic withholds assent

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: To say of what is that it is, and of what is not that it is not, is true -- truth is in the judgment.

positions.name: Protagoras
positions.claim: 'Man is the measure of all things' -- things are as they appear to each, relativizing truth.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Truth is the adequation of intellect and thing, grounded ultimately in the divine intellect.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Truth is agreement of knowledge with its object, but we know objects only as they appear.

positions.name: James
positions.claim: An idea is true insofar as it works, proving itself in the course of experience.

ideas.example: William James unsettled the tradition by making truth a matter of 'cash value'—an idea is true insofar as believing it works and leads us rightly through experience.

quotes.text: Man is the measure of all things.
quotes.context: The founding statement of relativism: things are to each person as they appear to that person. Plato's reply in the Theaetetus is that the doctrine undercuts itself, since it makes its own denial equally true.

ideas.name: Tyranny
ideas.gist: Lawless rule for the ruler's own sake.
ideas.framing: Tyranny is the corrupt rule of one who governs for his own interest, lawlessly and by force, against the good of the ruled. The archetypal bad regime, it defines by contrast what legitimate authority and the rule of law must be.
senses: The perversion of monarchy (one ruling for himself)
Lawless, arbitrary rule (unbound by law or consent)
Despotism (ruling free men as a master rules slaves)
The 'tyranny of the majority' (a modern extension)

disputes.q: What makes rule tyrannical -- who rules or how?

sides.view: The selfish, lawless end, not the number of rulers -- so even the many can be tyrants
The usurpation or illegitimacy of a single ruler

disputes.q: May a tyrant be resisted or killed?

sides.view: Tyranny forfeits authority; tyrannicide can be just
Resistance breeds worse disorder; endure or restrain by lawful means

disputes.q: Can tyranny take modern, softer forms?

sides.view: Only overt despotism is tyranny
Majorities and administrative power can tyrannize over mind and custom

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: The tyrant is the least happy of men -- a slave to his own lawless desires, the soul in worst disorder.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Tyranny is the worst constitution, the perversion of kingship -- ruling for the tyrant's good by force and fear.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Since the tyrant governs against the common good, his rule lacks true authority and may be resisted.

positions.name: Tocqueville
positions.claim: Warns of a new 'tyranny of the majority' and a mild but all-encompassing administrative despotism.

topics: Tyranny and the rule of law
ideas.example: Plato paints the tyrant as the unhappiest man alive—ruler of a city but slave to his own appetites, feared by all and trusting no one.

quotes.text: The tyrant is the least free of men.
quotes.context: The Republic's final argument that justice pays. Having power over everyone, the tyrant is enslaved by his own lawless appetites and can trust no one -- his outward mastery conceals total inner disorder.

ideas.name: Universal and Particular
ideas.gist: The general kind and the individual instance.
ideas.framing: The universal is what can be common to many (man, red, triangle); the particular is the individual, this one here. Their relation -- whether universals are real, mental, or mere words -- is the 'problem of universals' that divides the whole tradition.
senses: The universal as a real Form apart from things
As a common nature in things
As a concept in the mind
As a general name; the particular as the concrete individual

disputes.q: Do universals exist, and how?

sides.view: Real and separate, before the thing (ante rem)
Real but only in things (in re)
Only names or concepts, after the thing (post rem)

disputes.q: What is known -- universals or particulars?

sides.view: Science is of the universal; the particular as such is not known
Only particulars are real objects of knowledge

disputes.q: How is the individual individuated?

sides.view: Matter individuates the common form
A unique 'thisness' (haecceity) individuates

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: Universals are eternal Forms; particulars are real only by participating in them.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: The universal exists in particulars and is abstracted by intellect; only individuals subsist.

positions.name: Ockham
positions.claim: Only individuals exist; universals are natural signs in the mind, not things.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: The common nature exists in individuals and is universalized by the mind; matter individuates.

topics: Universals ante rem, in re, post rem
ideas.example: Ockham's razor cuts against Plato's Forms: why posit a realm of universals when only individual things exist and 'humanity' is just a name we apply to many?

quotes.text: Thisness.
quotes.context: His term (haecceity) for whatever makes an individual this one and no other. Species and form are shared; something further must account for singularity itself.

ideas.name: Virtue and Vice
ideas.gist: Excellence and defect of character.
ideas.framing: Virtue is excellence of character -- the settled disposition to be and do good; vice is its corruption. What the virtues are, whether they can be taught, and whether they suffice for the good life form the core of moral philosophy.
senses: Excellence of any kind (arete) vs. specifically moral virtue
Moral virtues (of character) vs. intellectual virtues (of mind)
The cardinal virtues and the theological virtues
Virtue as a mean; vice as excess or defect

disputes.q: Can virtue be taught?

sides.view: Virtue is knowledge, hence teachable
It comes by habit and practice, not teaching alone
It is a gift of grace or nature

disputes.q: Is virtue one or many?

sides.view: The virtues are one -- to have one is to have all, since all are wisdom
The virtues are distinct

disputes.q: Is virtue sufficient for happiness?

sides.view: Yes -- virtue alone makes the happy life
No -- some external goods are also needed

positions.name: Socrates
positions.claim: Virtue is knowledge; no one does wrong willingly, so vice is a kind of ignorance.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Moral virtue is a settled disposition to choose the mean, formed by habit and guided by practical wisdom.

positions.name: The Stoics
positions.claim: Virtue is the only good, sufficient for happiness; the passions are to be overcome.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Adds the theological virtues -- faith, hope, charity, infused by grace -- to the cardinal virtues.

positions.name: Hume
positions.claim: Virtues are qualities useful or agreeable to ourselves or others, approved by moral sentiment.

key_texts.text: Hume, Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals

ideas.example: Socrates' paradox: no one does wrong willingly, since to truly know the good is to do it—vice, then, is a kind of ignorance rather than a free choice of evil.

quotes.text: We become just by doing just acts.
quotes.context: Moral virtue is not taught like geometry but acquired like a craft, by practice. This is why upbringing matters so much: habits formed young decide what later feels natural.

quotes.text: No one does wrong willingly.
quotes.context: The Socratic paradox. If we always pursue what seems good, wrongdoing is a failure of knowledge rather than of will -- which implies vice is ignorance and virtue can be taught.

ideas.name: War and Peace
ideas.gist: Organized violence between communities—and its cessation.
ideas.framing: War is organized armed conflict between communities; peace, the condition of concord and order. Whether war is natural or avoidable, whether it can be just, and how a lasting peace might be secured are questions of the gravest human weight.
senses: Armed conflict between states or peoples
The 'state of war' (a relation of hostility, even without fighting)
Just war vs. unjust war
Peace as the mere absence of war vs. the 'tranquillity of order'; perpetual peace as an ideal

disputes.q: Is war natural or contrary to nature?

sides.view: A permanent possibility rooted in human nature and scarcity
An aberration; peace is the natural and rational condition

disputes.q: Can war be just?

sides.view: Yes -- under just cause, right authority, and right conduct
War is beyond justice, or is always a crime

disputes.q: Can lasting peace be achieved?

sides.view: A federation of states under law could secure perpetual peace
Peace is only ever a pause between wars

positions.name: Thucydides
positions.claim: Exposes the harsh logic of power -- 'the strong do what they can, the weak suffer what they must.'

positions.name: Augustine
positions.claim: Even war is waged for the sake of peace; a just war requires just cause and rightful authority.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Sets the conditions of a just war -- legitimate authority, just cause, and right intention.

positions.name: Hobbes
positions.claim: Without a common power, men are in a war of all against all; peace requires the sovereign.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: Proposes 'perpetual peace' through republican constitutions and a federation of free states under law.

topics: The nature and causes of war
Peace as the tranquillity of order
War among nations and international law

key_texts.text: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War

ideas.example: Kant argued that republics, whose citizens bear war's costs, would tend toward peace—sketching a federation of free states as the road to ending war.

quotes.text: The strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.
quotes.context: From the Melian Dialogue, where Athens demands surrender from a neutral island. Thucydides reports it without comment; the Athenians who reason this way are destroyed in Sicily soon after.

ideas.name: Wealth
ideas.gist: The possession and production of external goods.
ideas.framing: Wealth is the abundance of goods and money -- the material means of life and power. What wealth is, how it is rightly acquired and used, and its place in the good life and the just society are questions of economics and ethics alike.
senses: An abundance of useful goods and property
Money or riches (a store of exchangeable value)
Natural wealth (goods for use) vs. artificial (money-making for its own sake)
Wealth as a means to the good life vs. as an end in itself

disputes.q: Is the pursuit of wealth natural and good, or corrupting?

sides.view: Providing the means of life is natural and limited; unlimited money-making is unnatural
The pursuit of wealth through exchange enriches all

disputes.q: What is the source and measure of wealth?

sides.view: The labor embodied in goods
Money and gold

disputes.q: How should wealth be distributed?

sides.view: By merit and law, through free exchange
Private accumulation is theft from labor -- abolish private property

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Distinguishes natural, limited household provision from unlimited money-making; condemns usury.

positions.name: Adam Smith
positions.claim: Wealth is the annual produce of a nation's labor; free exchange, guided by an 'invisible hand,' increases it for all.

positions.name: Marx
positions.claim: Capitalist wealth is accumulated from the surplus value of unpaid labor; private property should be abolished.

positions.name: The Gospels
positions.claim: Warn of the love of money as a root of evils, and of how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom.

topics: The acquisition of wealth (natural and unnatural)
The source and measure of value

key_texts.text: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations

ideas.example: Aristotle warned against chrematistics—wealth-seeking with no natural limit—since money, unlike food or shelter, tempts us to pursue it endlessly for its own sake.

quotes.text: Led by an invisible hand.
quotes.context: Used once, and modestly: a merchant preferring domestic industry for his own security promotes an end he did not intend. Smith, a moral philosopher, was not claiming markets are always self-correcting.

ideas.name: Will
ideas.gist: The power of rational choice and self-determination.
ideas.framing: The will is the power of rational choice -- by which we decide, consent, and commit ourselves to act. Whether the will is free, how it relates to reason and desire, and whether it can choose against the good are pivotal questions for ethics and theology.
senses: Rational appetite (the desire that follows reason's judgment)
The power of free choice (liberum arbitrium)
Sheer volition or self-determination
The will as distinct from -- and sometimes opposed to -- the intellect

disputes.q: Is the will free?

sides.view: Yes -- we are the undetermined authors of our choices
No -- the will is determined by motives, causes, or God
Freedom is acting from one's own nature without compulsion

disputes.q: Does intellect or will have primacy?

sides.view: The will follows the intellect's judgment of the good
The will is the higher, freer power

disputes.q: Can the will choose evil knowingly?

sides.view: No -- we will only under the aspect of good
Yes -- the will can perversely reject the known good

positions.name: Augustine
positions.claim: The will is free but, since the Fall, in bondage to sin, needing grace to will the good rightly.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: The will is rational appetite; it necessarily seeks the good in general but is free as to particular goods.

positions.name: Scotus
positions.claim: The will is self-determining and, in a sense, superior to the intellect (voluntarism).

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: A free, autonomous will legislating the moral law to itself is the ground of morality.

positions.name: Schopenhauer
positions.claim: Will is the blind, striving essence of the world, of which intellect is only the servant.

topics: The primacy of will or intellect

key_texts.text: Augustine, On Free Choice of the Will
Aquinas, Summa Theologica I QQ.82-83; I-II QQ.6-17
Kant, Groundwork; Critique of Practical Reason
Schopenhauer, The World as Will and Representation

ideas.example: Augustine agonizes that he commands his hand and it obeys, yet commands his will and it resists—the self strangely unable to simply will what it wills.

quotes.text: Grant what you command, and command what you will.
quotes.context: The prayer that provoked the Pelagian controversy. If we cannot obey without grace, is the will free? Augustine's answer -- that grace frees rather than overrides -- shapes the debate for centuries.

ideas.name: Wisdom
ideas.gist: Knowledge of the highest things, and how to live.
ideas.framing: Wisdom is the highest knowledge -- of first causes and of how to live well. It unites the theoretical grasp of ultimate things with the practical mastery of conduct, and is the very end that philosophy loves.
senses: Theoretical wisdom (sophia -- of first principles and highest things)
Practical wisdom (phronesis or prudence -- knowing how to act)
Wisdom as a gift of God (in Scripture)
Wisdom vs. mere cleverness or learning

disputes.q: Is wisdom theoretical or practical?

sides.view: Contemplation of the highest truths is its peak
Wisdom is chiefly knowing how to live

disputes.q: Is wisdom human or divine?

sides.view: The philosopher can attain it
Only God is wise; humans merely love wisdom

disputes.q: Can wisdom be taught?

sides.view: It can be cultivated and learned
Even the wise cannot simply transmit it

positions.name: Socrates
positions.claim: Knows that he knows nothing; human wisdom begins in recognizing one's own ignorance.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: Distinguishes theoretical wisdom (of first causes) from practical wisdom (right deliberation about action).

positions.name: The Stoics
positions.claim: The sage is wholly governed by reason and virtue, indifferent to fortune.

positions.name: Aquinas
positions.claim: Wisdom judges all things by the highest cause, God; it is both a virtue and a gift.

key_texts.text: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI; Metaphysics I

ideas.example: The oracle called Socrates wisest, and he agreed only in this: others thought they knew what they didn't, while he alone knew the extent of his own ignorance.
ideas.hook: Knowing the highest things, and how to live.

quotes.text: I know that I know nothing.
quotes.context: His gloss on the oracle that called him wisest. He knows less than he is credited with, but unlike others he knows that -- human wisdom begins in recognizing the limits of one's knowledge.

ideas.name: World
ideas.gist: The ordered whole of all that is.
ideas.framing: The world is the ordered whole of all that is -- the cosmos. Ideas about it swing between order and chaos, eternity and creation, one world or many, and whether it is intelligible, good, and made for a purpose.
senses: The physical universe or cosmos
An ordered whole (kosmos = order)
The totality of finite things, as against God
The plurality of worlds

disputes.q: Did the world have a beginning?

sides.view: The world is eternal
The world was created and began
Reason cannot decide (antinomy)

disputes.q: Is there one world or many?

sides.view: One unique, finite cosmos
Infinitely many worlds

disputes.q: Is the world ordered by design or chance?

sides.view: The cosmos is a work of intelligence and providence
Order arises from the chance motion of atoms

positions.name: Plato
positions.claim: The Timaeus depicts a craftsman shaping the cosmos on eternal models -- an ordered, ensouled whole.

positions.name: Aristotle
positions.claim: One eternal, finite cosmos, moved from beyond by the unmoved mover.

positions.name: Lucretius
positions.claim: Infinite worlds form and dissolve by the chance concourse of atoms.

positions.name: Augustine
positions.claim: God freely created the world, and time with it, out of nothing.

positions.name: Kant
positions.claim: The world-whole is an idea of reason; claims about its bounds fall into antinomies.

topics: The origin of the world (eternity vs. creation)
The order and design of the cosmos
The extent and shape of the universe
The end or destiny of the world

key_texts.text: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things

ideas.example: Plato's Timaeus depicts the cosmos as the work of a craftsman shaping chaos toward the good—the world as ordered artifact, not random heap.
ideas.hook: All that is, as one order.

quotes.text: The best of all possible worlds.
quotes.context: Not a claim that nothing is bad. A perfect God choosing among possible worlds must choose the one whose overall richness and order is greatest -- which may require particular evils. Voltaire's Candide mocks the doctrine rather than refuting it.

Adam Smith.name: Adam Smith
Adam Smith.role: Scottish moral philosopher and political economist
Adam Smith.note: Founded modern economics, showing how the division of labor and free exchange, guided as if by an invisible hand, enlarge a nation's wealth.
Adam Smith.works: The Wealth of Nations (1776); The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759)

Anaxagoras.name: Anaxagoras
Anaxagoras.note: Introduced Mind (nous) as the ordering principle that sets an original mixture in motion -- the first appeal to intelligence as a cosmic cause.

Anselm.name: Anselm of Canterbury
Anselm.note: Coined 'faith seeking understanding' and devised the ontological argument, reasoning from the concept of God to God's existence.

Aquinas.name: Thomas Aquinas
Aquinas.role: Dominican friar and theologian at Paris and Naples
Aquinas.note: Synthesized Aristotle with Christian doctrine, holding faith and reason distinct but harmonious. His treatment of law, virtue, God and the soul is the tradition's most systematic.
Aquinas.works: Summa Theologica; Summa Contra Gentiles; On Kingship

Archimedes.name: Archimedes
Archimedes.role: Greek mathematician and engineer of Syracuse
Archimedes.note: Founded statics and hydrostatics -- the law of the lever and the principle of buoyancy -- uniting mathematics with physical machines.
Archimedes.works: On the Equilibrium of Planes; On Floating Bodies

Aristotle.name: Aristotle
Aristotle.role: Greek philosopher, student of Plato, tutor of Alexander
Aristotle.note: Brought the Forms down into things as their form and end, and founded logic, biology and systematic ethics and politics. The single most-cited voice in the tradition.
Aristotle.works: Metaphysics; Physics; Nicomachean Ethics; Politics; On the Soul; Poetics

Augustine.name: Augustine of Hippo
Augustine.note: Fused Platonism with Christianity, made the inward self a philosophical subject, and framed evil as privation, time as a puzzle of the soul, and history as two cities.
Augustine.works: Confessions; City of God; On Free Choice of the Will

Austin.name: John Austin
Austin.note: Founded legal positivism: law is the command of a sovereign backed by sanction, and its existence is one thing, its merit another.

Bacon.name: Francis Bacon
Bacon.role: English statesman and philosopher of science
Bacon.note: Called for a new method of systematic observation and induction, so that knowledge might extend human power -- nature is commanded by being obeyed.
Bacon.works: Novum Organum (1620); The Advancement of Learning

Beccaria.name: Cesare Beccaria
Beccaria.note: Argued punishment is justified only to deter, should be the mildest sufficient, prompt and certain -- and never capital.

Bentham.name: Jeremy Bentham
Bentham.role: English jurist and founder of utilitarianism
Bentham.note: Made the greatest happiness of the greatest number the standard of law and morals, and proposed to measure pleasures and pains directly.
Bentham.works: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789)

Berkeley.name: George Berkeley
Berkeley.note: Denied matter altogether: sensible things are collections of ideas, and to be is to be perceived.
Berkeley.works: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge (1710)

Boethius.name: Boethius
Boethius.role: Roman senator and philosopher, executed for treason
Boethius.note: Wrote in prison the Consolation of Philosophy, whose solution to foreknowledge and freedom -- that God sees all time at once -- became standard.

Bradley.name: F. H. Bradley
Bradley.note: Located moral obligation concretely in 'my station and its duties' rather than in abstract rules.

Burke.name: Edmund Burke
Burke.note: Founded modern conservatism by defending custom and prescription as the accumulated wisdom of generations against abstract revolutionary reason.
Burke.works: Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790)

Cantor.name: Georg Cantor
Cantor.note: Made the actual infinite mathematically respectable, proving there are different sizes of infinity and founding set theory.
Cantor.works: Contributions to the Founding of the Theory of Transfinite Numbers (1895)

Carnap.name: Rudolf Carnap
Carnap.role: German-American philosopher of the Vienna Circle
Carnap.note: Held that metaphysical statements are literally meaningless because unverifiable, and sought to rebuild knowledge on logic and observation.
Carnap.works: The Logical Structure of the World (1928)

Cicero.name: Cicero
Cicero.note: Transmitted Greek philosophy to Rome and to the Latin West, and gave the natural-law tradition its classic statement: one eternal law, the same for all peoples.
Cicero.works: On Duties; On the Laws; On the Commonwealth

Claude Bernard.name: Claude Bernard
Claude Bernard.note: Founded experimental medicine, insisting on controlled experiment and the constancy of the body's internal environment.
Claude Bernard.works: Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine (1865)

Comte.name: Auguste Comte
Comte.role: French philosopher, founder of positivism and sociology
Comte.note: Held that humanity passes through theological, metaphysical and positive stages, and that science alone yields real knowledge.

Condorcet.name: Marquis de Condorcet
Condorcet.note: Wrote, while in hiding from the Terror, the classic statement of the indefinite perfectibility of the human mind.
Condorcet.works: Sketch for a Historical Picture of the Progress of the Human Mind (1795)

Copernicus.name: Nicolaus Copernicus
Copernicus.note: Placed the sun at the center and set the earth in motion, beginning the revolution that displaced humanity from the middle of the cosmos.
Copernicus.works: On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres (1543)

Darwin.name: Charles Darwin
Darwin.note: Explained the diversity of life by descent with modification through natural selection, and placed man within the same continuum as the other animals.
Darwin.works: On the Origin of Species (1859); The Descent of Man (1871)

Democritus.name: Democritus
Democritus.note: With Leucippus held that all that exists is atoms moving in the void, and that sensible qualities like color and sweetness are conventions rather than features of things.

Descartes.name: Rene Descartes
Descartes.note: Rebuilt knowledge from the one thing he could not doubt -- that he was thinking -- and split reality into thinking mind and extended matter.
Descartes.works: Discourse on Method (1637); Meditations on First Philosophy (1641)

Dewey.name: John Dewey
Dewey.role: American pragmatist philosopher and educational reformer
Dewey.note: Treated experience as the organism's active transaction with its environment, and education as growth through doing rather than absorbing.
Dewey.works: Democracy and Education (1916); Experience and Nature (1925)

Empedocles.name: Empedocles
Empedocles.role: Greek philosopher and poet of Acragas
Empedocles.note: Proposed the four roots -- earth, air, fire, water -- mixed and separated by Love and Strife, an early attempt to explain change without denying being.

Epicurus.name: Epicurus
Epicurus.role: Greek philosopher, founder of the Garden at Athens
Epicurus.note: Taught an atomism with a swerve to save freedom, and a hedonism aimed at tranquility -- freedom from bodily pain and mental disturbance, not indulgence.

Euclid.name: Euclid
Euclid.note: His Elements organized geometry into definitions, postulates and demonstrations, and became the model of rigorous knowledge for two thousand years.

Frege and Russell.name: Gottlob Frege & Bertrand Russell
Frege and Russell.note: Recast logic in symbolic form capable of expressing relations and generality, vastly extending what Aristotle's syllogism could capture.
Frege and Russell.works: Frege, Begriffsschrift (1879); Russell & Whitehead, Principia Mathematica (1910-13)

Freud.name: Sigmund Freud
Freud.note: Made the unconscious central to mind, traced love to the sexual drive sublimated into higher aims, and read religion as illusion.
Freud.works: The Interpretation of Dreams (1900); Civilization and Its Discontents (1930)

Galen.name: Galen
Galen.role: Greek physician to the imperial court
Galen.note: Systematized the medicine of the humors, whose balance is health; his authority dominated medicine until the Renaissance.

Galileo.name: Galileo Galilei
Galileo.note: Turned the telescope on the heavens and mathematized motion, insisting nature's book is written in mathematics. Condemned by the Inquisition in 1633.
Galileo.works: Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632); Two New Sciences (1638)

Hegel.name: G. W. F. Hegel
Hegel.note: Made contradiction the engine of development, and read history as the progressive self-realization of freedom in the consciousness of Spirit.
Hegel.works: Phenomenology of Spirit (1807); Philosophy of Right (1821)

Heraclitus.name: Heraclitus
Heraclitus.note: Taught that all things flow and that strife is the father of all -- reality is process, held together by an underlying logos. The great ancient champion of change against Parmenides.

Hippocrates.name: Hippocrates
Hippocrates.note: Insisted diseases have natural rather than divine causes and that the physician assists nature; his name attaches to the oath binding doctors to do no harm.
Hippocrates.works: Airs, Waters, Places; Aphorisms; the Hippocratic Oath

Hobbes.name: Thomas Hobbes
Hobbes.role: English philosopher, writing through the Civil War
Hobbes.note: Derived politics from matter in motion and appetite: without a common power life is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short, so men covenant to erect an absolute sovereign.

Horace.name: Horace
Horace.note: His verse letter on poetry gave later ages the formula that the poet aims to instruct and to delight, and the demand for disciplined craft.

Hume.name: David Hume
Hume.note: Traced all ideas to impressions, showed that no reasoning justifies our expectation that the future will resemble the past, and made custom the great guide of life.
Hume.works: A Treatise of Human Nature (1739); Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748)

James.name: William James
James.note: Founded pragmatism -- an idea is true insofar as it works -- and treated religion by its fruits in lived experience.
James.works: The Principles of Psychology (1890); Pragmatism (1907); Varieties of Religious Experience (1902)

Jefferson.name: Thomas Jefferson
Jefferson.note: Drafted the Declaration of Independence and distinguished a natural aristocracy of virtue and talent from an artificial one of birth and wealth.
Jefferson.works: Declaration of Independence (1776); Notes on the State of Virginia

Kant.name: Immanuel Kant
Kant.note: Argued the mind supplies the forms that make experience possible, limiting knowledge to appearances, and grounded morality in a categorical imperative binding rational wills.
Kant.works: Critique of Pure Reason (1781); Groundwork (1785); Critique of Judgment (1790)

Kepler.name: Johannes Kepler
Kepler.note: Replaced circles with ellipses and found the laws of planetary motion, completing the Copernican revolution mathematically.

Lamarck.name: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck
Lamarck.note: Proposed the first systematic theory of evolution, driven by use, disuse and the inheritance of acquired characteristics.

Laplace.name: Pierre-Simon Laplace
Laplace.note: Pushed mechanical determinism to its limit: an intelligence knowing all forces and positions could see the whole future -- and had no need of the hypothesis of God.
Laplace.works: Celestial Mechanics; A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities (1814)

Later methodologists.name: Later philosophers of science
Later methodologists.note: Argued science advances not by simple induction but by proposing bold conjectures and testing them severely against experience.

Lavoisier.name: Antoine Lavoisier
Lavoisier.role: French chemist, guillotined in the Terror
Lavoisier.note: Overturned phlogiston, named oxygen, and established that matter is conserved through chemical change -- founding modern chemistry.

Leibniz.name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
Leibniz.note: Co-invented the calculus and argued that nothing is without a sufficient reason, that substance is force, and that this is the best of all possible worlds.

Locke.name: John Locke
Locke.note: Denied innate ideas, deriving all knowledge from experience, and grounded government in consent and the protection of life, liberty and property.
Locke.works: Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689); Two Treatises of Government (1689)

Lucretius.name: Lucretius
Lucretius.note: Put Epicurus into verse to free men from fear of gods and death, arguing the soul is atoms that scatter -- so death is nothing to us.

Machiavelli.name: Niccolo Machiavelli
Machiavelli.note: Severed political prudence from Christian virtue, asking what actually preserves a state rather than what ought to.

Maimonides.name: Moses Maimonides
Maimonides.role: Jewish philosopher, jurist and physician of Cordoba and Cairo
Maimonides.note: Guarded God's transcendence by insisting we can say only what God is not, and treated prophecy as a natural perfection of intellect and imagination.
Maimonides.works: Guide for the Perplexed; Mishneh Torah

Marx.name: Karl Marx
Marx.note: Read history as driven by material conditions and class struggle, and analyzed capitalist wealth as accumulated surplus taken from labor.

Michels.name: Robert Michels
Michels.note: Formulated the iron law of oligarchy: even avowedly democratic organizations tend to fall under the control of a few.

Mill.name: John Stuart Mill
Mill.note: Refined utilitarianism by ranking higher pleasures above lower, and defended liberty on the ground that society may restrain us only to prevent harm to others.
Mill.works: On Liberty (1859); Utilitarianism (1863); A System of Logic (1843)

Milton.name: John Milton
Milton.note: Dramatized the fall of angels and men, and argued in prose for free speech and the liberty of conscience.

Modern liberalism.name: Modern liberalism
Modern liberalism.role: The tradition running from Locke through Mill and beyond
Modern liberalism.note: Holds that individuals possess rights prior to the state, which exists to secure them and is limited by them.

Montaigne.name: Michel de Montaigne
Montaigne.note: Invented the essay as self-examination, using the diversity of human customs to puncture the assumption that our own habits are nature's law.

Montesquieu.name: Montesquieu
Montesquieu.note: Classified governments by their animating principles and argued liberty depends on separating legislative, executive and judicial power.

Newton.name: Isaac Newton
Newton.note: United heaven and earth under three laws of motion and universal gravitation, and professed to frame no hypotheses beyond the phenomena.

Ockham.name: William of Ockham
Ockham.note: Denied that universals exist outside the mind and urged that explanations not multiply entities beyond necessity -- the razor that bears his name.

Parmenides.name: Parmenides
Parmenides.role: Philosopher of Elea, founder of the Eleatic school
Parmenides.note: Argued that being simply is -- ungenerated, indivisible, unchanging -- and that change and plurality are illusions of the senses. Sets the permanence side of the tradition's oldest quarrel.

Pascal.name: Blaise Pascal
Pascal.role: French mathematician, physicist and religious thinker
Pascal.note: Founded probability theory, then turned to defending faith -- portraying man as a thinking reed, wretched and great, suspended between beast and angel.

Pelagius.name: Pelagius
Pelagius.note: Denied inherited sin and insisted the will is free to keep God's law -- the position against which Augustine defined original sin and grace.

Pico della Mirandola.name: Pico della Mirandola
Pico della Mirandola.note: His Oration made man the one creature without a fixed nature, free to shape himself toward beast or angel -- the manifesto of Renaissance humanism.
Pico della Mirandola.works: Oration on the Dignity of Man

Plato.name: Plato
Plato.role: Athenian philosopher, student of Socrates, founder of the Academy
Plato.note: Held that the changing things we see imitate eternal Forms, knowable by reason. His dialogues set the agenda for nearly every idea in this index.
Plato.works: Republic; Phaedo; Symposium; Timaeus; Theaetetus; Laws

Plotinus.name: Plotinus
Plotinus.note: Derived all reality by emanation from a single ineffable One, through Intellect and Soul -- the bridge between Plato and Christian theology.

Polybius.name: Polybius
Polybius.role: Greek historian taken hostage to Rome
Polybius.note: Explained Rome's success by its mixed constitution, balancing consuls, senate and people, and described the cycle by which constitutions decay.

Protagoras.name: Protagoras
Protagoras.role: The most famous of the Sophists
Protagoras.note: His dictum that man is the measure of all things made him the ancestor of relativism, and Plato's recurring opponent on truth and knowledge.

Pseudo-Dionysius.name: Pseudo-Dionysius
Pseudo-Dionysius.role: Anonymous Syrian theologian writing under an apostolic name
Pseudo-Dionysius.note: Set out the celestial hierarchy of angels and the negative way of speaking about God, shaping medieval mysticism.
Pseudo-Dionysius.works: The Celestial Hierarchy; The Divine Names

Ptolemy.name: Ptolemy
Ptolemy.role: Greek astronomer and geographer at Alexandria
Ptolemy.note: His geocentric system of epicycles predicted the planets accurately enough to govern astronomy for fourteen centuries.

Quintilian.name: Quintilian
Quintilian.note: Defined the orator as the good man skilled in speaking, binding eloquence inseparably to character and civic duty.

Rawls.name: John Rawls
Rawls.note: Revived systematic political philosophy with justice as fairness -- principles chosen behind a veil of ignorance. A modern extension beyond Adler's 1952 set.

Rousseau.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
Rousseau.note: Held that man is born free yet is everywhere in chains, that legitimate rule expresses the general will, and that civilization has corrupted natural goodness.
Rousseau.works: The Social Contract (1762); Emile (1762); Discourse on Inequality (1755)

Russell.name: Bertrand Russell
Russell.role: British philosopher, logician and public intellectual
Russell.note: Helped found modern logic and analytic philosophy, and argued much traditional metaphysics dissolves under logical analysis.
Russell.works: Principia Mathematica (1910-13); The Problems of Philosophy (1912)

Schopenhauer.name: Arthur Schopenhauer
Schopenhauer.note: Held that behind appearances lies a blind, striving Will, of which the intellect is merely the servant -- the root of philosophical pessimism.
Schopenhauer.works: The World as Will and Representation (1818)

Scotus.name: John Duns Scotus
Scotus.note: Argued for the primacy of the will over intellect, and coined 'thisness' (haecceity) as the principle making each individual uniquely itself.

Sidney.name: Philip Sidney
Sidney.note: Defended poetry as teaching virtue more movingly than philosophy or history, by joining precept to living example.

Socrates.name: Socrates
Socrates.role: Athenian philosopher, executed by the city
Socrates.note: Wrote nothing, but by relentless questioning turned philosophy toward how one ought to live. His claim that virtue is knowledge, and that he knew only his own ignorance, shapes everything after.

Spinoza.name: Baruch Spinoza
Spinoza.role: Dutch philosopher, expelled from his synagogue
Spinoza.note: Identified God with Nature -- one infinite substance -- and treated the emotions as following necessary laws, so that freedom comes through understanding.

The Federalist.name: The Federalist authors
The Federalist.role: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay
The Federalist.note: Argued for the proposed U.S. Constitution, showing how checks, balances and an extended republic could restrain both tyranny and majority faction.

The Gospels.name: The Gospels
The Gospels.role: The four canonical accounts of the life of Jesus
The Gospels.note: Their teaching on love, poverty and the kingdom reshaped Western thought about charity, wealth, humility and the neighbor.

The Romans.name: The Roman jurists
The Romans.role: The lawyers and codifiers of Roman law
The Romans.note: Built citizenship into a legal status with defined rights extendable across an empire, and left the vocabulary of Western law.
The Romans.works: the Digest; the Institutes of Justinian

The Sophists.name: The Sophists
The Sophists.role: Itinerant teachers of rhetoric and success in Greek cities
The Sophists.note: They drew the great antithesis between nature (physis) and convention (nomos), arguing much of morality is merely customary -- the provocation to which Socrates and Plato reply.

The Stoics.name: The Stoics
The Stoics.role: School founded by Zeno of Citium; later Seneca, Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius
The Stoics.note: Held that the cosmos is a rational, providential whole, that virtue alone is good, and that freedom lies in accepting what is not up to us.
The Stoics.works: Epictetus, Discourses; Marcus Aurelius, Meditations; Seneca, Letters

The modern synthesis.name: The modern synthesis
The modern synthesis.role: The union of Darwinian selection with genetics
The modern synthesis.note: Showed how heredity supplies the variation on which natural selection acts, resolving the chief objection to Darwin.

The tragedians.name: The Greek tragedians
The tragedians.note: The Athenian dramatists staged the collisions of fate, law, family and the gods, giving the tradition its most powerful images of necessity and human limit.
The tragedians.works: Oresteia; Antigone; Oedipus the King; Bacchae

The utilitarians.name: The utilitarians
The utilitarians.note: Made the greatest happiness of the greatest number the test of every law, institution and act.

Thrasymachus.name: Thrasymachus
Thrasymachus.note: In Plato's Republic he presses the hardest challenge to justice -- that it is merely whatever serves the interest of the stronger.

Thucydides.name: Thucydides
Thucydides.note: Wrote the first rigorously causal history, stripped of myth, as a possession for all time -- and the founding text of political realism.

Tocqueville.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
Tocqueville.role: French aristocrat, magistrate and observer of America
Tocqueville.note: Judged democratic equality providential and just, yet warned of the tyranny of the majority and a mild, all-embracing administrative despotism.

Tolstoy.name: Leo Tolstoy
Tolstoy.note: Judged art by the sincerity of the feeling it transmits and its service to human brotherhood, condemning much celebrated art as counterfeit.
Tolstoy.works: War and Peace (1869); What Is Art? (1897)

Vico.name: Giambattista Vico
Vico.note: Argued we can know history because men made it, and that nations pass through recurring ages of gods, heroes and men.

William James.name: William James
William James.note: Founded pragmatism -- an idea is true insofar as it works -- and treated religion by its fruits in lived experience.
William James.works: The Principles of Psychology (1890); Pragmatism (1907); Varieties of Religious Experience (1902)
